articles.title: Israel relembra as vítimas do ataque terrorista de 7 de Outubro | G1
articles.standfirst: Atentado realizado pelo grupo terrorista Hamas em território israelense há exatos 3 anos deixou quase 1.200 mortos e 251 reféns. Manifestações nesta quarta (7) ocorre a poucas semanas das eleições parlamentares em Israel.
articles.summary: Atentado realizado pelo grupo terrorista Hamas em território israelense há exatos 3 anos deixou quase 1.200 mortos e 251 reféns. Manifestações nesta quarta (7) ocorre a poucas semanas das eleições parlamentares em Israel.
articles.body:
Israelenses relembram vítimas do ataque terrorista de 7 de Outubro em manifestação em Jerusalém, em Israel, em 7 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Ammar Awad

Israel homenageia nesta quarta-feira (7) as vítimas do ataque perpetrado há três anos pelo grupo terrorista palestino Hamas , pouco antes de eleições marcadas pela lembrança do dia mais sangrento desde a criação do Estado de Israel .

Em Reim, onde em 7 de outubro ocorria o festival de música eletrônica Nova —invadido ao amanhecer por milicianos islamistas—, familiares das vítimas fizeram um minuto de silêncio às 0h29, no horário de Brasília (6h29 no fuso local), o horário exato em que começou o ataque a partir de Gaza.

"Foi o minuto em que nossas vidas mudaram para sempre", disse à agência de notícias AFP Katia Zohar, mãe de Bar, assassinada aos 23 anos junto com outras 360 pessoas naquele festival, a poucos quilômetros da Faixa de Gaza.

"Lembro de tudo", acrescentou. "Do momento em que ela me ligou para que eu fosse buscá-la, porque havia mísseis voando (...), e depois quando ligou da estrada, gritando que estavam atirando nela".

"Sinto muita falta dele", afirmou Anna Davitashvili, de 53 anos, lembrando-se de seu filho mais velho, Shaun, morto aos 25 anos junto com amigos no festival Nova.

"Sinto uma dor imensa por não ter conseguido salvá-lo", contou, com lágrimas nos olhos.

Um minuto de silêncio também foi observado no kibutz Kfar Aza, perto da fronteira com Gaza, onde 64 pessoas foram assassinadas e 18 sequestradas durante o fatídico ataque.

Na manhã de sábado, 7 de outubro de 2023, coincidindo com um feriado judaico, centenas de combatentes palestinos cruzaram a fronteira após dispararem uma intensa salva de foguetes a partir de Gaza.

Armados com fuzis e granadas, eles massacraram famílias em comunidades agrícolas e atacaram delegacias e bases do exército, em um dia que deixou 1.221 mortos, segundo um levantamento da AFP baseado em dados oficiais israelenses.

Ação em praia em Tel Aviv, em Israel, relembra vítimas do ataque terrorista de 7 de Outubro no 3º aniversário do atentado, em 7 de outubro de 2026. Junto com representações para cada israelense morto, está escrito: 'O preço do fracasso. 1.163 mortos e 251 reféns'. — Foto: Aviv Atlas via REUTERS

Imagem aérea de drone mostra fonte em Tel Aviv, em Israel, com água tingida de vermelho para simbolizar vítimas do ataque terrorista de 7 de Outubro de 2023, no dia em que o atentado completou 3 anos. — Foto: REUTERS/Avishai Reisner

Os membros do Hamas também fizeram 251 reféns e os levaram para Gaza; 44 deles já estavam mortos.

O Hamas , que permanece presente em Gaza apesar das promessas incessantes de Netanyahu de eliminar o movimento, divulgou um comunicado apresentando o 7 de outubro como "um dia glorioso na história do nosso povo".

O movimento afirmou ter "derrubado o mito do exército invencível" e declarou que a ofensiva de um ano atrás foi "a resposta natural e a culminação de décadas de sofrimento amargo".

As cerimônias ganham uma dimensão especial este ano por serem as primeiras desde a entrada em vigor, em outubro do ano passado, do cessar-fogo em Gaza.

O território palestino ficou reduzido a escombros e mergulhado em uma imensa crise humanitária após mais de dois anos de hostilidades israelenses, que deixaram mais de 74.000 mortos, segundo dados das autoridades do Hamas , considerados confiáveis pela ONU.

As cerimônias oficiais foram realizadas em Jerusalém na segunda-feira, data definida pelo governo de acordo com o calendário hebraico. O primeiro-ministro, Benjamin Netanyahu , participou dos eventos.

Os atos ocorrem sob segurança reforçada, a três semanas das eleições gerais em Israel e uma semana após a tentativa frustrada de ataque contra um avião com destino a Tel Aviv.

O ministro da Defesa de Israel , Israel Katz, anunciou na terça-feira que o exército estava em alerta devido a informações "de inteligência sobre as intenções do Hamas de tentar realizar ataques e operações terroristas" por ocasião do aniversário.

Segundo as autoridades do enclave palestino, pelo menos duas pessoas morreram em ataques israelenses noturnos contra o território.

As eleições de 27 de outubro serão as primeiras desde os ataques.

As pesquisas preveem uma disputa difícil para o primeiro-ministro Netanyahu que, nos últimos três anos, também lançou ofensivas em larga escala no Líbano e no Irã, além de ter intervindo na Síria e no Iêmen.

Um de seus rivais é Naftali Bennett, ex-primeiro-ministro que o critica por não ter evitado os ataques.

"Isso foi um fracasso colossal do Estado de Israel , que foi fundado para defender os judeus em nossa terra", declarou a jornalistas no local do festival Nova.

articles.title: Comissária viaja por estados para estocar remédio do filho | G1
articles.standfirst: Thais Jucá e o marido, de Vinhedo (SP), reuniram quase 50 caixas do Depakote Sprinkle após a fabricante anunciar o fim da comercialização no Brasil; família teme interrupção do tratamento do filho de 4 anos.
articles.summary: Thais Jucá e o marido, de Vinhedo (SP), reuniram quase 50 caixas do Depakote Sprinkle para o filho de 4 anos após a fabricante anunciar o fim da comercialização no Brasil.
articles.body:
Vinhedo (SP): mãe comissária viaja por estados para estocar remédio de epilepsia do filho que deixará de ser vendido — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

A comissária de bordo Thais Jucá, de Vinhedo (SP), aproveita as viagens de trabalho para visitar farmácias em outros estados e comprar um remédio para epilepsia que deixará de ser comercializado no Brasil.

Com medo de interromper o tratamento do filho de 4 anos, ela e o marido, o engenheiro elétrico João Jucá, conseguiram reunir quase 50 caixas do medicamento Depakote Sprinkle em pouco mais de um mês.

A corrida da família pelo produto começou após a farmacêutica Abbott notificar que a fabricação e a importação do remédio seriam encerradas definitivamente em 2026 por motivações comerciais (veja a nota abaixo) .

A maior dificuldade enfrentada pelos pais é a falta de opções no mercado nacional com o mesmo formato de administração, chamado de "sprinkle". O medicamento é essencial para crianças ou pessoas com dificuldade de engolir porque:

é composto por microgrânulos armazenados dentro de cápsulas;

pode ser aberto para que os grânulos sejam misturado a alimentos pastosos, como iogurte;

evita a necessidade de ingestão de comprimidos grandes, que não podem ser mastigados ou triturados.

"Fomos procurar algo alternativo e não tem no Brasil esse tipo de administração de remédio, que são microgrânulos. Ele é pequeno, ele não engole um remédio, existe uma alternativa, só que a alternativa é um comprimido grande. Ele não pode ser mastigado, ele não pode ser dissolvido", relata João.

Depakote Sprinkle: família de Vinhedo (SP) estoca medicamento para epilepsia que será descontinuado — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Para evitar a descontinuidade dos tratamentos, a Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária ( Anvisa ) determina que a fabricante mantenha o mercado devidamente abastecido pelo período de 12 meses . Apesar de terem garantido o remédio para um ano, João e Thais esbarram na data de validade dos produtos estocados e aguardam uma solução.

"Desesperador, porque você já passa por todo o diagnóstico, pela internação, pela UTI, pelo desespero de ter o filho nessa situação que a gente não imaginava. E aí quando você encontra uma saída, quando as coisas vão voltando ao normal, a rotina, você fala, eu tenho meu filho de volta? Não tenho. É muito difícil", desabafa Thais.

A mudança abrupta na medicação de pacientes com a doença controlada pode trazer riscos. O neurologista Willian Ferreira, do Vera Cruz Hospital, alerta que a adaptação do paciente envolve a tolerabilidade ao formato exclusivo . "O ideal é procurar uma avaliação precoce com o neurologista que acompanha para definir um novo plano terapêutico", orienta.

"[No caso do Depakote] o grânulo dessa substância fica armazenado dentro dessa cápsula, então é passível de a gente partir essa cápsula e administrar junto a um alimento pastoso, um iogurte, então facilita muito bem essa questão da adesão também do paciente, principalmente nessa faixa etária mais pediátrica das crianças".

"A forma como o paciente se adapta com a medicação, não é apenas o mecanismo de ação, a substância em si, mas a tolerabilidade principalmente. Existe uma série de questões de tentativas prévias do paciente, às vezes o paciente não tolerou a formulação cápsula, então isso acaba realmente trazendo uma série de inseguranças para os pais", completa o médico.

A Anvisa informou que não possui instrumento legal que impeça os laboratórios farmacêuticos de retirarem seus medicamentos do mercado. Pontuou, porém, que as empresas devem comunicar a descontinuação definitiva ou temporária de fabricação ou importação de medicamentos com pelo menos 180 dias de antecedência, devendo assegurar o fornecimento normal do produto durante esse período.

Por se tratar do único medicamento comercializado contendo um princípio ativo importante, a empresa deverá, manter o mercado devidamente abastecido pelo período de 12 meses. Essa medida tem como finalidade assegurar aos pacientes tempo hábil para a realização de eventuais ajustes de dose ou para a adequada adaptação ao tratamento com seus médicos, evitando descontinuidade terapêutica.

Caso a empresa não cumpra o prazo estabelecido pela regulamentação aplicável, podem ser adotadas as medidas administrativas e legais cabíveis, visando assegurar a continuidade do tratamento e o adequado abastecimento do mercado.

A farmacêutica Abbott informou que a decisão pela descontinuidade do medicamento não está ligada à qualidade, segurança ou eficácia e que as unidades atualmente disponíveis no mercado podem ser usadas normalmente até o final do respectivo prazo de validade.

Disse ainda que pacientes e familiares que tiverem dúvidas sobre o tratamento devem conversar com seus médicos sobre alternativas terapêuticas disponíveis no Brasil para manutenção do tratamento.

articles.title: Programa de estágio convoca mais de 2,3 mil universitários na Bahia | G1
articles.standfirst: Lista foi divulgada nesta quarta-feira (7), no site da Seab. Convocados deverão acessar o site para verificar os procedimentos, prazos e documentação.
articles.summary: Lista do Partiu Estágio foi divulgada nesta quarta-feira (7), no site da Seab. Convocados deverão acessar o site para verificar os procedimentos, prazos e documentação.
articles.body:
Convocados no programa Partiu Estágio — Foto: Ascom/Saeb

Mais de 2,3 mil universitários foram convocados nesta quarta-feira (7) para o programa Partiu Estágio. A lista de convocados foi publicada no site da Secretaria da Administração (Saeb).

Os selecionados para as vagas vão receber uma mensagem via WhatsApp, informando alteração do seu status no site do Governo da Bahia. Na sequência, eles deverão acessar o site para verificar os procedimentos, prazos e documentação.

Depois disso, os estudantes relacionados deverão entrar em contato com a unidade de recursos humanos do órgão onde irão atuar entre os dias 13 e 23 de outubro.

Dos 2.384 estudantes selecionados, 1.191 irão atuar na capital baiana e os outros 1.193 em cidades da Região Metropolitana de Salvador e do interior do estado.

As vagas vão preencher 53 órgãos estaduais, situados em 152 diferentes municípios baianos. As graduações com maior número de vagas são administração (423), pedagogia (245) e direito (192).

articles.title: Trabalhadores são resgatados em situação análoga à escravidão em Moju | G1
articles.standfirst: Grupo de 11 pessoas dormia em barraco de palha e bebia água em embalagem de água sanitária. Entre resgatados de carvoaria estão dois adolescentes de 15 e 17 anos.
articles.summary: Grupo de 11 pessoas dormia em barraco de palha e bebia água em embalagem de água sanitária. Entre resgatados de carvoaria estão dois adolescentes de 15 e 17 anos.
articles.body:
Auditores-fiscais do trabalho resgataram 11 trabalhadores de situação considerada análoga à escravidão em uma carvoaria em Moju , no nordeste do Pará.

Segundo os auditores-fiscais, os trabalhadores não tinham carteira assinada e viviam na área do local onde trabalhavam. O flagrante foi divulgado na terça-feira (6), mesmo dia que o governo federal atualizou a “lista suja” do trabalho escravo .

Eles dormiam em oficina de máquinas e em barraco de palha, bebiam água guardada em embalagem de água sanitária e tomavam banho em igarapé.

Segundo a Superintendência Regional do Trabalho no Pará, os trabalhadores estavam em condições análogas à escravidão em uma carvoaria na zona rural do município, às margens da PA-151.

Todos os trabalhadores são moradores de Breu Branco e trabalhavam produzindo carvão vegetal de madeira nativa. Entre os resgatados, há dois adolescentes, de 15 e 17 anos.

As atividades na carvoaria foram interrompidas imediatamente e os responsáveis terão de indenizar os trabalhadores resgatados.

articles.title: Carrie: Is Prime Video's adaptation still relevant in 2026?
articles.summary: Another beloved classic gets a modern-day twist. Its cast and creator argue why it needed to be remade.
articles.body:
Adaptations, remakes and reboots are all the rage right now, and there’s often one question that crops up - why?

See also "what's the point?" and "do we need another one?" whenever a story is resurrected from the past.

Carrie, Prime Video's new TV series based on Stephen King's debut novel, has been no exception.

It's not the first time the tale of high school bullies and supernatural powers has been adapted for the screen.

Director Brian de Palma's 1976 movie version is a horror classic, with some of its most famous scenes and imagery widely considered iconic within the genre.

But the cast and creator of the latest version, which drags Carrie's story forward 50 years into a world of social media, have been telling BBC Newsbeat why they believe it's still relevant in 2026.

Fans of the novel have been quick to complain the new version of Carrie is not "book accurate", pointing out that she was originally an abrasive, even unlikeable character.

In the TV adaptation, Carrie has been raised behind closed doors by her paranoid father and deeply religious mother, and only enters school after a tragedy reveals her existence to authorities.

Audiences see a different version of the character in the show - one who's naive, but open and eager to learn new things.

"There's a lot of opinions, and I purposely avoided the original movie and and the book before filming because I hadn't seen it or read it," Summer H Howell, who plays Carrie, tells Newsbeat.

"And I wanted to create this new, light version of Carrie that was excited to get out of her house and just curious about the world and people."

However, the 22-year-old actress says the journey her character goes on is not so different, and argues it's still relevant today.

"It's the story of an outsider, and bullying has not gone away in 50 years," she says.

"If anything, it's just gotten worse with social media."

Social media plays a huge part in the adaptation by horror director Mike Flanagan, who's best known for series such as The Haunting of Hill House.

In his version of Carrie, some of the most famous scenes, including the dramatic prom moment, are adapted to a world where everything is filmed and shared online.

Alison Thornton, who plays chief bully Chris Hargensen, says social media "is kind of a villain in the show".

"You can post something, or someone will take a video of something, and the fact that it can be permanently online is actually quite terrifying," she says.

Thornton says the adaptation aims to show how online posts can have "repercussions in real life".

Showrunner Flanagan tells Newsbeat it would have been "impossible to ignore the impact social media has had in changing the way we see each other".

Fifty years ago, he says, bullying would have been relatively "private", and confined to "the classroom, in the halls, in the school".

"It's happening with the audience of the entire digital world and enshrined forever, permanently on these platforms.

"It's a whole different ball game that way," he says.

Carrie is the latest project from Prime Video targeted at Gen Z viewers based on a popular novel.

The Summer I Turned Pretty , Your Fault: London , and Off Campus have been huge hits for the streamer, and it's leaned into trends such as BookTok to generate interest in the shows.

Josie Totah, who plays Chris's sidekick Tina, agrees remakes and adaptations are popular, but says she would only get involved with one if the "intention" felt right.

"No one wants to just remake something for the sake of remaking it," she says.

"'Why now?' - unless that can be answered thoroughly, I don't think that I would want to do it."

There are worries from fans that revisiting existing works leaves less space for original stories.

Totah says projects such as this year's indie horror hit Obsession also deserve to be championed.

"Those are equally as important as the ones that we've already told in the past, if not maybe a little bit more," she says.

So far, Flanagan's version of Carrie has had a mostly positive response from critics, with an 85% positive rating on review website Rotten Tomatoes.

Most praised the performances and social commentary, although some reviewers felt it wasn't as scary as earlier versions and accused it of sanding down some of the original characters' harder edges.

The verdict from fans remains to be seen.

Flanagan hasn't just expanded on the original story, but has also made some fairly major changes, possibly laying the ground for further series to be made.

"I try to think about how fans will feel because I'm a Stephen King fan first," he says.

"So I have very strong opinions about changes that are made in adaptation."

Flanagan has brought other Stephen King novels to the screen before, but those have tended to be much more faithful to the source material.

Some of his best-known projects, reinventions of The Haunting of Hill House by author Shirley Jackson and The Fall of the House of Usher by Edgar Allan Poe, have been based on works by long-deceased authors.

"I've just never done this with an author who's still alive or one with whom I already have a very intensely productive working relationship," he says.

"I hope people are going to look at these changes and say: 'Oh, this is actually why it makes good sense to tell this story again today'."

Carrie will launch on Prime Video on 7 October

articles.title: From warships to container ships: Why India & US are putting shipbuilding back in focus
articles.summary: Both India and the United States are ramping up their shipbuilding capability at a moment when China's share of global ship manufacturing has effectively
articles.body: Both India and the United States are ramping up their shipbuilding capability at a moment when China's share of global ship manufacturing has effectively overtaken the rest of the world combined. According to the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, China's share of global shipbuilding output rose from under 5% in 2000 to more than 53% in 2025, while the US accounted for just 0.11 percent in 2024, and effectively nothing by 2025. What makes this particularly significant is that the same Chinese yards, workers and suppliers building commercial tankers also produce destroyers, aircraft carriers and submarines for the PLA Navy, with China State Shipbuilding Corporation alone turning out more commercial tonnage annually than the entire American shipbuilding industry has produced since the Second World War.This scale of dominance has become a genuine strategic concern for New Delhi, and a response is now taking shape. India currently accounts for less than 1% of global shipbuilding output, with an official target of breaking into the world's top ten shipbuilding nations by 2030, and the top five by 2047. The country operates 61 shipyards in total, eight under the central government, two with state governments and 51 in the private sector. In 2025, the government approved a Rs 69,725 crore package to revitalise the sector, built around a Rs 24,736 crore shipbuilding financial assistance scheme, a Rs 25,000 crore maritime development fund, and a Rs 19,989 crore shipbuilding development scheme aimed at pushing domestic capacity to 4.5 million gross tonnes annually. Output has already risen 41%, from 40,923 gross tonnage in 2024 to 57,637 gross tonnage in 2025, with average contract values more than quintupling in the same period. For context, UN trade and development (UNCTAD) puts global annual ship production at over 6 million gross tonnes.India's naval shipbuilding capability is already considerably more mature than its commercial side. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said in June 2026 that more than 40 indigenously built warships and submarines had been inducted into service in recent years, with 45 major platforms currently under construction. The Project 17A frigate programme has involved over 200 Indian MSMEs and achieved roughly 75% indigenous content, and construction timelines are genuinely improving, INS Mahendragiri's launch-to-delivery period was cut from 63 months to 31, while the fifth P17A frigate, INS Dungarpur, was delivered after an 80-month build, down from 93 months for the class's first ship. Hindustan Shipyard's upgraded Slipway-4 and a new 300-tonne Goliath crane now allow construction of vessels up to 45,000 DWT, including the Navy's 43,500-tonne Fleet Support Ships.The commercial shift is becoming visible too, particularly at Cochin Shipyard. In February 2026, it signed a contract with French shipping major CMA CGM for six 1,700-TEU LNG-fuelled feeder container ships, its first order from a global liner operator, worth around $300 million. CSL has since deepened its international partnerships further, including an Rs 1,800 crore joint venture with DP World's Drydocks World Dubai to jointly operate an international ship repair facility in Kochi, India's first such public-private collaboration, positioning Kerala as a potential global ship repair hub. GRSE, long dependent almost entirely on warship orders, has diversified as well, with non-defence work now making up 20-25% of its order book, up from roughly 5% five years ago, including a contract for 12 vessels for a German commercial customer.Even so, India remains nowhere close to China's scale, and the more useful comparison may be with the United States itself, which is grappling with a strikingly similar problem despite operating the world's most advanced navy. Washington's own commercial shipbuilding base has hollowed out so significantly that it announced plans for a fifth public Navy shipyard in August 2026, its first in over 80 years, while actively exploring foreign shipbuilding partnerships to rebuild lost capacity. What India doesn't need to do is replicate China's entire industrial system. A commercially competitive shipbuilding sector, one building tankers, container ships and offshore platforms, would almost automatically deepen the industrial base the Navy itself draws on. For India, the lesson from both Beijing and Washington is essentially the same: naval power ultimately rests on industrial depth, not simply the number of ships already afloat.

articles.title: Nearly 3 in 4 Pakistan inmates await trial amid prison overcrowding in country: Report
articles.summary: Pakistan's prisons are facing severe overcrowding, with people awaiting trial making up nearly three-fourths of the country's prison population, a Human
articles.body: Pakistan's prisons are facing severe overcrowding, with people awaiting trial making up nearly three-fourths of the country's prison population, a Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) report has found.The report, 'Beyond the Prison Wall: Reducing Overcrowding in Pakistan's Prisons', said 73.41% of inmates were under-trial in 2024. The share has gone up from 66% in 2017, The Express Tribune reported.The report said Pakistan's prisons were operating at 152.2% of their approved capacity on average during July and August 2024.The HRCP said simply building more prisons would not address the problem. It pointed to delays in the justice system, including lengthy trials, weak bail procedures and the widespread use of pre-trial detention.Punjab faces an even bigger problem. According to official figures cited by the HRCP, 74,773 prisoners were held in 45 prisons across the province in September 2026. The sanctioned capacity was 39,204, meaning the prisons were operating at nearly 191% of capacity.Of the total inmates, 54,932 were awaiting trial.Punjab has added new prisons, barracks and other facilities over the years, but the report said the additional capacity has not matched the rise in the number of prisoners.The scale of the problem has grown majorly. Punjab province had 52,803 prisoners against a capacity of 21,527 in 2010. Overcrowding in the province stood at 173.6% in 2024, according to figures cited by The Express Tribune.The HRCP blamed arbitrary arrests, delays in investigations and lengthy prosecution for the growing number of people held without conviction.As a result, many accused people remain behind bars for months or even years while waiting for investigations and court proceedings to move forward, the report said.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I am Omer': Former Hamas hostage reflects on surviving 505 harrowing days in captivity
articles.summary: Omer Shem Tov revealed the 505 days he spent as a Hamas hostage in Gaza, from total darkness in a tiny cage to refusing orders under threat of death.
articles.body: On Oct. 6, 2023, Omer Shem Tov and his family were celebrating his mother's birthday. Less than 24 hours later, Hamas terrorists kidnapped Shem Tov from the Nova Music Festival and held him hostage in Gaza for 505 days. Nearly three years later, Shem Tov is telling his story while trying to regain his sense of self. In a conversation with Fox News Digital, Shem Tov recalled that when Hamas' attack started at 6:29 a.m. on Oct. 7, 2023, people at the festival took precautions, but were not panicked. He explained that "in Israel, we're very used to it." Thinking that the aerial attack was the only thing coming, festival goers, including Shem Tov and his friends, began packing up and heading to their cars to drive home. However, many of them never made it home and, as in Shem Tov's case, some came back much later. In his book, "Light From the Darkness," Shem Tov recounts his experience of the attacks and throughout his time as a hostage in Gaza. He also opened up about having taken ecstasy shortly before the attacks began. ISRAELI MEDICAL WORKERS WHO TREATED OCT 7 WOUNDED RELIVE DAY TERROR HIT HOME "In my book, I talk about it, first of all, very openly, because I mean I want people to understand that I'm just like any other 20-year-old," Shem Tov told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to party. I wanted to have fun." Shem Tov explained to Fox News Digital that he felt that the ecstasy, combined with his adrenaline, actually helped him "run faster and without stopping" as the attack began. He said that the feeling disappeared suddenly as terrorists got closer and began firing at him and his friends. Hours after being taken into Gaza, Shem Tov felt the effects again. He said it was "a very scary feeling." The first 50 days of his captivity were spent in total darkness, in a cage so small he could not stand up or spread out his arms. Shem Tov, who is an asthmatic, said he had trouble breathing in the tiny space and that he was "starved in the most extreme way." "I was in complete darkness, I couldn't see anything, and I just went crazy," Shem Tov told Fox News Digital, adding that in his mind, he was blaming God and "everyone else" for what had happened. "After a week, I got to a point where I realized that God has created me with the power of free will. I can choose to do whatever I want. I can choose to believe, I can choose not to believe. I can choose between good and bad and evil." FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL "I realized that I have two choices: Either I sink into depression and I blame everyone and God for everything that happened to me and I just sink deeper and deeper until eventually I think that I would have just died of depression and broken heart, or either I look at the situation, and I try to make something good in some way out of it," he said. While in complete darkness, Shem Tov said he was "crying to God" and telling Him, "God, from now on I trust you and I know that I'm in the right place, in the right time. This is exactly where I am supposed to be, and I'm in your hands from now on. Do as you wish, do as you will." "From that moment on, I just saw light. I really did see light in complete darkness," he added. While in captivity, Shem Tov faced extreme pressure from his captors, yet he refused to break even under the threat of death. When they ordered him to detonate traps against advancing Israel Defense Forces soldiers, he flatly refused. Even when his captors threatened to shoot him on the spot, Shem Tov held his ground and dared them to pull the trigger. ISRAEL'S NEW EXHIBIT EXPOSES YEARS OF HAMAS TERRORIST PLANNING BEFORE OCT 7 MASSACRE "There was some kind of red line that I cannot cross. I will just, I will not do it," Shem Tov told Fox News Digital. "If I wasn't in captivity, maybe I would be up there. Maybe I would fight for my brothers and my sisters that were hostages. So, that was my red line and I just couldn't do it, and I preferred to die than do it." On Feb. 22, 2025, after enduring 505 days as a hostage, Shem Tov returned to Israel in a prisoners-for-hostages exchange between Israel and Hamas and was reunited with his family. He spent months advocating for the hostages still left in the Gaza Strip. The last of the living hostages were released on Oct. 13, 2025. Shem Tov still travels to tell his story and speaks out against what he sees as a dangerous narrative gap in how the war is portrayed abroad. Recently, he wrote an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal criticizing a controversial documentary called "NAZA," the Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage." The film depicts casualties in Gaza and received a 25-minute standing ovation at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. Shem Tov did not mince words when criticizing the film. "It felt like 25 minutes of a rain of knives that just stabbed me," he told Fox News Digital. "The war in Gaza was horrible, horrible for both sides, but in the movie 'NAZA' they only showed one side. They didn't show my side. What about me? I was NAZA. I was collateral damage." OPINION: THE WORLD IS DEBATING SANCTIONS AGAINST ISRAEL. I AM WATCHING YOUNG WARRIORS REBUILD THEIR LIVES When reached for comment, representatives for the team behind "NAZA" referred Fox News Digital to previous statements made by directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. During a Q&A following the North American premiere of NAZA, which took place at the 64th New York Film Festival, Abraham addressed the criticisms of the film, calling the Oct. 7 attacks "unjustified," while arguing that the barbarism of that day could not be used to defend Israel's actions. "I think it's important for me to say that, you know, it's in the film, and it's — completely unjustified, the massacre of October the 7th, but it also cannot justify what you've seen in the film, doesn't justify the slaughter of so many civilians in Gaza, the massacres at food sites," Abraham said. "When I was looking at those trucks, I thought, like, I don't want to live in a world where empathy, rightful empathy to Israeli victims is weaponized by leaders like Netan — you know, cynical people who promise nothing other than perpetual occupation and war, is weaponized to mean a lack of empathy to Palestinians," he continued. Abraham was referring to protest trucks outside the screening that showed images of Oct. 7. MS RACHEL CALLS GAZA JOURNALIST ‘FRIEND’ IN RESURFACED CLIP AFTER HE ADMITS HIDING OCT 7 HOSTAGE FOOTAGE Shem Tov, however, maintains that the film's framing erases the reality of what happened during the Oct. 7 attacks and what brought the war to Gaza in the first place. He told Fox News Digital that he witnessed Hamas deliberately weaponizing the suffering of both the hostages and Palestinians as means of propaganda. "They don't really care about who dies," Shem Tov said of Hamas. "For them, the more dead, the better." "Seeing a standing [ovation] of 25 minutes was just, well, I can't explain how hurtful it was, how hurtful it was. Not seeing me, not seeing the true reason of what's happening there. And I mean, I think people just should know more, should learn more, should see more," he added. Since his release from captivity, Shem Tov has witnessed this ideological divide firsthand while speaking at college campuses. He said that his visit to Columbia University was particularly triggering, as he had seen the encampments and people clad in keffiyehs on TV while he was being held hostage. "It's sad that people are following trends in some ways," he told Fox News Digital. "Most of the students get their information from social media, and on social media, you can see a lot of lies, a lot of propaganda, and I think they should open a book. They should read more. They should learn more." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Three years after he was taken from the Nova festival, Shem Tov continues to tell his story while also looking towards the future. He told Fox News Digital that, while he has embraced what he sees as a duty to tell his story for all those who cannot tell their own, he will not let the 505 days he spent as a hostage define his life. "I have my duty and I know what's my duty, and I will do anything to complete my job, but I'm much more than this, I am Omer."

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden airport
articles.summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the escalation deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body: CAIRO — Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the escalation deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but did not provide evidence. Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform. Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases, Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen. The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels. On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait. The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 30 miles south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government. Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m. (7 p.m. Tuesday ET). The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said. Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government. “The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” the Aden police said in a statement. The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said. Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware. The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah. “The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis.

articles.title: Students are not anti-socials, can protest genuine concerns at designated spot, not by blocking roads: Bombay HC
articles.summary: MUMBAI: “They are students, not anti-socials’’ the Bombay high court observed orally while hearing a plea against the weeklong ongoing protests by
articles.body: MUMBAI: “They are students, not anti-socials’’ the Bombay high court observed orally while hearing a plea against the weeklong ongoing protests by thousands in Pune against alleged malpractices in the Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) examinations.The HC said students have a right to protest if there are genuine causes, .The HC bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said Pune is an educational hub and students “are not keen to come on roads to agitate. If they are , it would mean the grievances are serious.’’The HC said students work hard to appear for public service examinations and if they “find any hanky panky in the procedure, they have a right to protest.’’The HC also said there should be fairness in public recruitment examinations like the one held by the MPSC and students had a right to protests but they cannot block roads.While one group of students withdrew their stir, for other two the HC said they can apply for permission and change of venue which the State can then consider.The HC said students’ genuine demands be heard and sought a reply on steps taken from the State in three weeks. The reply should state department-wise vacancies. The bench saidThe State Advocate General Milind Sathe said on September 30 Maharashtra government had met and accepted 3 out of 4 main demands the students had.The first one asking for resignation of the MPSC chief Vivek Bhimanwa, the State cannot by law grant, but the State has already written to the Governor to look into the complaints made against him.A petition by Amit Supekar and another resident of Pune to seek a designated space for staging agitations and sought immediate stoppage and legal action against protestors for conducting three illegal simultaneous protests at SM Joshi Bridge, Alka Talkies Chowk and Ahilya Study Centre.The protests had begun after an MPSC examination conducted for the Drug Controller post and it was found that three days earlier, the paper had been leaked online.The students had felt that FIRs are not enough and heads must roll, hence they demanded resignation of the MPSC chief.The HC however asked students to withdraw any blocking of roads and said any prolonged stir could affect their own career paths.The CJ said Pune is known as an academic city. He said to the State, “if the students have a genuine demand, you must look into it.’’“See the plight of the parents who have sent their children to study in Pune. These children are innocent. All parents in the country are in crisis,...No message should go across the country that it is not a fit place for students, or the parents will also have their apprehension,’’ the bench said orally, expressing concern and said it would ensure the recruitment drive is taken care of and maintains fairness.The HC wants the State to inform of the steps it has taken and intends to to tackle the issue.The AG Sathe said the second demand of having 2 mega recruitment for 70000 posts also has been accepted as were two other demands of having Rs 100 as exam fees, like Rajasthan has and to make the examination offline.Pune is the State’s second largest city with a population of 70 lakh the advocate for the petitioner argued and said the protestors were blocking roads. Some protestors denied they were blocking roads.The students’ lawyer said police had given permission to hold protests on October 2 after the Ganesh festival at a particular location.The AG said after the meeting with the government, protestors had agreed to withdraw but continued and at present no permission exists for any protests and if they apply afresh for another location, such plea would be considered.“So far as affairs of MPSC are concerned, State has appointed a committee to look into it,’’ the AG said.For removal of the MPSC chief, the AG said law prescribes a process that includes an inquiry.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Ted Lasso's Hannah Waddingham to star in Gavin and Stacey's duo's The Choir
articles.summary: Ruth Jones and James Corden's new show also stars X-Men's James McAvoy and Harry Potter's Jim Broadbent.
articles.body:
Gavin and Stacey co-creators Ruth Jones and James Corden have revealed details about their new TV comedy drama series The Choir.

The eight-episode show will air on Apple TV and feature guest appearances by Ted Lasso's Hannah Waddingham, X-Men's James McAvoy and Harry Potter's Jim Broadbent.

The series follows brother Ben (Corden) and sister Lisa (Jones), who have not seen each other for several years.

The pair previously said the idea came from their family connection to choirs , with Corden's mum and Jones' sister both members of one.

Ben has been living abroad, while Lisa has continued living in their small town where "nothing ever happens".

But when events take a sorry turn, Ben is forced to return to "a life he never wanted, a town he never liked and a family from which he's estranged".

The cast includes Tom Davis, Rosie Sheehy, Susan Brown, Jason Watkins, Alexandira Riley, Sylvestra Le Touzel, Tom Edden, Gary Lamont, Emily Lloyd-Saini, Stephen Leask, Luiis Rouf, Jo Foster, Evie Jones and Farrah Abbassy.

Jones and Corden are executive producers for the series, which is now in production and set to air in 2027.

Jones previously said: "We both feel that choirs, amateur choirs especially, bring people together in a way that maybe nothing else does.

"There was just this idea to bring this group of characters together from different backgrounds, all sorts of different things going on in their lives."

Corden added they wanted "to try and make a show about community and the importance of community".

"It's just about a group of people that come together every week and enjoy and sing, and it's really about the life that's within that," he added.

When Jones and Corden first met in 2000, they never imagined it would lead to 22 episodes of a record-breaking TV show.

The pair were filming Fat Friends at the Crowne Plaza in Leeds and formed an unexpected friendship.

They then co-wrote Gavin and Stacey, in which they played Vanessa "Nessa" Jenkins and Neil "Smithy" Smith, the best friends of the title characters

The hit comedy ran for three series, and three Christmas specials, between 2007 and 2024.

Their memoir was published on 9 October - almost a year on from the show's record-breaking finale on Christmas Day 2024.

Alongside their new collaboration, Jones recently appeared in new Netflix series Run Away - based on the Harlan Coben novel.

She has also teamed up with Steve Speirs in a six-part comedy series called Better Later, about the challenges of relationships in middle age.

Jones recently portrayed Mrs Bennet in another comedy series, The Other Bennet Sister, which was inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, while Corden has just finished a stint on Broadway.

articles.title: France halts police use of stun grenades at student protests
articles.summary: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to make public address after thousands rally to demand more funding for education.
articles.body:
France has temporarily banned police from using stun grenades at student-led protests , the interior minister said, amid growing accusations of police brutality following several days of student demonstrations nationwide.

The announcement on Wednesday came a day after hundreds of thousands of students and supporters marched across France to demand more funding for education and better conditions in high schools, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to convene an emergency meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and other key ministers to try to defuse the crisis.

Lecornu will make a public address later on Wednesday on the school protests as well as the country’s finances, his office said.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told radio broadcaster RTL early on Wednesday that he had suspended police use of stun grenades at the protests.

A 15-year-old lost a hand in the northern city of Lens on Monday after police fired a stun grenade.

Earlier, a 14-year-old student was hit in the face by a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged on Tuesday over the incident in the capital, Paris.

Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Nunez said.

Rights groups, students and parents’ groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

The Ministry of the Interior said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began last month, the overwhelming majority of them minors.

More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the Ministry of Justice said, without specifying the crimes.

At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu’s office.

Protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages and demands for more funding for education.

Parents, teachers and union workers joined the demonstrations in Paris and other cities on Tuesday amid accusations that police were using disproportionate force.

Sporadic violent clashes have broken out between police and protesters at what otherwise have been largely peaceful demonstrations.

Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told lawmakers that it would not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.

articles.title: Drumcree: Garvaghy Road dispute could lead to issues with marches in other areas, say residents
articles.summary: There have been 11 days of deadlock between Garvaghy Road residents and the local Orange Order over the proposed march in Portadown, County Armagh.
articles.body:
A stand-off over a decision to allow a parade down a predominantly nationalist road could lead to issues with Orange Order marches in other areas, according to a residents' group.

There have been 11 days of deadlock between Garvaghy Road residents and the local Orange Order over the proposed march in Portadown, County Armagh.

The Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) met 11 nationalist residents' groups on Wednesday. Afterwards, Linda O'Neill of the GRRC said: "This is no longer just about the Garvaghy Road."

Earlier, it emerged Oasis' Noel Gallagher, Oscar winner Susan Sarandon and Line of Duty star Adrian Dunbar were among dozens to sign a letter in support of residents.

Other people to have signed the letter supporting residents in the Drumcree dispute include musician Paul Weller, Derry Girls star Siobhán McSweeney and The Smiths' Johnny Marr.

On Wednesday, residents from the Garvaghy Road met groups including the Bogside Residents Association in Londonderry, and the Lower Ormeau Concerned Community, and Crumlin Road and Ardoyne Residents Association, both of which are in Belfast.

In a statement last month , the groups expressed their full support for the Garvaghy Road residents.

They said they had developed "accommodations" around Orange parades in their respective areas over time.

The statement last month added: "Our concern is that such accommodations could unravel if the Orange Order continue to insist on parading down Garvaghy Road, or indeed pursue the same demands in other nationalist/Catholic areas."

On Wednesday, O'Neill said: At the minute the support from all over Ireland, particularly all of the other communities in the north of Ireland coming here and supporting us, are propping up our community right now; we have never seen support and solidarity like it.

"The Orange Order needs to take responsibility, and so do the Parades Commission for making this issue bigger than the Garvaghy Road, this is no longer just about the Garvaghy Road, this is about all of us."

Solicitor Pádraig Ó Muirigh said the meeting had been organised as an "act of solidarity and support" for the Garvaghy residents from residents who are "dealing with similar disputes across the country".

He said that many were concerned the progress that had been made over the years regarding marches might unravel due to the "recklessness of the Orange Order and the ineptitude of the parades commission".

Speaking at a separate press conference, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said they would "not be bullied or threatened by any residents' group who step outside the law".

He said he was "very confident" in the support across Northern Ireland for their march adding "there's no threat to our parades. They're legal".

"My message to the real residents of Garvaghy road is [that] I understand the pressure you're under.

"People came into your part of the town...unasked for, unwanted and it's time they left, and left the residents in peace, and perhaps a resolution could be resolved."

Earlier on Wednesday, the Orange Order said that the "lawful 35 continue to stand ready to exercise the legal right" they "have established for the first time in 28 years".

"We once more urge the PSNI to actually take positive steps to implement the determination. We have seen no such proper efforts being made, and in due course, a court will also have to scrutinise this."

"We will not give up that legal right, as to do so would be to legitimise mob rule. We will continue our dignified, peaceful and lawful stand."

The letter backing the Garvaghy Road residents was addressed to Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant and urged him to work with the Irish government to appoint an "independent international mediator" to "facilitate a robust, durable solution".

Dexy's Midnight Runners frontman Kevin Rowland, who also signed the letter, told BBC News NI that it "originated from an honest response to the situation on the Garvaghy Road".

"The letter speaks for itself. It came about from conversations from those of us looking on from afar.

"It was an organic process inspired by the courage of the residents.

"As concerned individuals, we are not seeking to build an organisation or alternative platform to the voices of the residents. We would only wish to amplify their voices."

Others among the 48 signatories include Trainspotting writer Irvine Welsh, movie director Ken Loach, Graham 'Suggs' McPherson from Madness, Kneecap, Imelda May, Maxine Peake and trade unionist Mick Lynch.

The Northern Ireland Office (NIO) confirmed it had received the letter and said the secretary of state continued to engage with all parties for a resolution.

Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin clashed with Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald in the Dáil (lower house of Irish parliament) over the Drumcree parading dispute on Wednesday.

McDonald urged him to "apply all necessary pressure" on the UK government to end the "dangerous limbo and stalemate" over the Orange Order march.

The taoiseach said the situation in Portadown was "not as simplistic" as McDonald had suggested - and accused her of using the issue for "electoral reasons".

Martin said he has "remained in contact" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in recent days and expressed hope for a "mediated resolution".

There has been more than a week of deadlock in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, 27 September.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.

The stand-off has caused considerable political fallout in Northern Ireland, with First Minister O'Neill facing a vote of no confidence over her involvement in the protest.

The vote is due to fail due to it requiring cross-community support at the Northern Ireland Assembly.

Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry .

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal is considering its ruling in a legal challenge brought by the residents to block the march going ahead.

articles.title: DANNY DANON: From Oct 7 to Flight 1073: The resilience that keeps Israel standing
articles.summary: Israeli Ambassador Danny Danon says Oct. 7, Flight 1073 and the hostage fight show Israel’s enemies failed to break its spirit.
articles.body: Among the passengers of FlyDubai Flight 1073 on Sept. 30 were Israelis returning to Israel to mark the third anniversary of Oct. 7. Little did they know, their flight nearly became one of the worst terrorist attacks in Israel’s history. Three years ago, on Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terrorists launched the deadliest attack on the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Hamas stormed across Israel’s border, slaughtering roughly 1,200 people, murdering families in their homes and young people at a music festival. They took 251 men, women and children hostage into Gaza. HAMAS ALLEGEDLY BUILT WEAPONS DEPOTS ACROSS EUROPE, PLANNED TERROR ATTACKS AS OCT 7 ANNIVERSARY NEARED Oct. 7 was not simply an attack on Israel. Hamas sought to shatter Israel’s sense of security, terrorize Jews around the world and destroy the possibility of a different Middle East. They wanted to turn the Arab world against Israel and make peace between Israel and its neighbors impossible. Documents captured by the IDF in the Gaza Strip show that Hamas closely monitored efforts to advance normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia. Oct. 7 was meant, in part, to derail that process. Hamas succeeded in delaying it, but it failed to destroy the broader framework of peace and cooperation that Israel had built with its Arab neighbors. Three years later, Flight 1073 was another attempt to strike at that same reality. The idea that an Israeli family could board a plane in Dubai on a Jewish holiday and fly home to Israel was once unimaginable. Today, it is part of a new Middle East, one in which Israelis and Arabs travel, trade and build relationships across borders. That is precisely the reality that terrorism sought to destroy. As Flight 1073 flew over Saudi Arabia, its terrorist co-pilot stabbed the captain and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. He sent the plane into a drastic dive, with the apparent intention of crashing the aircraft and its 174 passengers into Ben Gurion International Airport. WHEN HATE BECOMES A BUSINESS: THE MONETIZATION OF ANTISEMITISM Neither Oct. 7 nor Flight 1073 could break the Israeli spirit of resilience. On the morning of Oct.7, Israeli civilians left their homes and fought Hamas terrorists with their bare hands to protect their families and communities. On Flight 1073, heroic passengers likewise rushed the cockpit, putting their own lives on the line to stop the terrorist and save everyone on board. They were defending more than themselves. They were defending the possibility of a different future, one in which Israel is secure, connected to its neighbors and at peace. We have continued to see this Israeli resilience in the years following October 7. Israel has rebuilt its security posture. Hamas has been severely weakened, Hezbollah’s military capabilities have been substantially degraded, and Israel has established new security realities in Gaza and along its northern border. The threats have not disappeared, but the strategic environment Israel faces today is fundamentally different from the one it faced three years ago. We also never stopped fighting for our hostages. Three years after Oct. 7, they all came home. Our efforts included bringing former captives to the United Nations Security Council to advocate for the immediate release of the remaining hostages. In January, Israel announced that the final hostage, Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, had been identified and returned for burial. We thank the Trump administration for helping secure the deal that brought them all home. ISRAELI MEDICAL WORKERS WHO TREATED OCT 7 WOUNDED RELIVE DAY TERROR HIT HOME That is what Israeli resilience looks like. A nation that leaves nobody behind. A nation that could not begin to truly rebuild until all our hostages came home. Israel has also shown diplomatic resilience in the past three years. September marked six years since the Abraham Accords. Before the recent U.N. General Assembly, it was my honor to celebrate that milestone with distinguished officials from the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Kazakhstan as a prospective member. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Although we continue to face criticism over the war in Gaza, Israel remains deeply engaged with the world and is building new partnerships in the Middle East and beyond. Our history has taught us that resilience is not simply the ability to survive tragedy. It is the strength to rise from it, to rebuild and to choose life. We saw it in the aftermath of World War II. The survivors of the Holocaust dedicated their lives to rebuilding the Jewish state. Now, after Oct. 7, we see the same resilience: the resilience of the families who lost so much, yet found the strength to stand, rebuild and carry Israel forward. Resilience is part of our national DNA. Three years ago, on Oct. 7, Hamas tried to break us. They failed. They changed us, wounded us and left scars that will never fully heal. But they did not break us. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Not on Oct. 7, not in the skies above the Middle East and not ever.

articles.title: Christa Pike is awake after surviving execution: What happens now?
articles.summary: Tennessee death row inmate survives execution attempt, sparking legal and medical concerns.
articles.body:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived a failed execution by lethal injection in a US prison last week, is conscious and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers have said.

Fifty-year-old Pike was convicted of murdering her classmate in 1995.

The Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate ever to survive “after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs”.

Pike’s “unprecedented” survival raises questions about her medical and legal future.

Pike is under guard, recovering at a hospital in Nashville where she was rushed after surviving the lethal injection administered by the Tennessee Department of Correction. Her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at the hospital on September 30.

“Against all odds”, Pike is now “conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care”, her lawyers said, adding that “she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed”.

They called her recovery “medically unprecedented”.

Pike’s prognosis remained “unclear”, they said, adding that, at a minimum, she faced a lengthy recovery.

Fifty-year-old Pike was sentenced to death after being convicted of a murder as a teenager.

The case sparked debate over the death penalty for young offenders, as Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp in 1995.

Pike’s lawyers sought clemency, citing her age, childhood sexual abuse and mental health problems, including post-traumatic stress disorder.

The case had already attracted attention in the run-up to the execution date, as Pike would have been the first woman put to death by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years.

7:30pm – The attempt to execute Pike got under way on September 30 in the death chamber at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike was given a chance to make a final statement before two doses of the chemical pentobarbital were administered as executioners attempted to put her to death.

7:35pm – Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting.

8:53pm – Media were escorted out of the witness room.

9:14pm – An ambulance arrived at the prison to take Pike to hospital.

Journalists who witnessed the execution said a black curtain was drawn from inside the death chamber during the process to insert the intravenous lines into Pike, in line with state regulations. This is done to conceal the identities of the workers who perform the procedure.

Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the condemned person does not die after the first set. But there are no instructions for how to proceed if the person does not die after a second lethal injection dose.

Pike’s lawyers are due in court on Wednesday, where they will be seeking more information from the Tennessee Department of Correction about the botched execution attempt.

They are seeking a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.

Medical and lethal injection experts said it is possible there was a problem with the way the IV line was inserted, causing the drug to collect in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown,” Pike’s lawyers said in a court filing.

Prior to the execution attempt, Pike’s lawyers had requested her death penalty to be carried out by firing squad or hanging, because she had small veins and a blood-clotting condition called thrombocytosis. They feared the condition could make the insertion of intravenous needles difficult and increase the risk of a failed procedure.

Pike’s lawyers have called for her death sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole after the failed execution attempt.

What do Tennessee government officials say?

Republican Governor Bill Lee called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.

The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.

Frank Strada, the former commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, who was the prison chief at the time of Pike’s failed execution, agreed to step down later this month.

US Senator Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate to replace Bill Lee, called on Tennessee to explore other methods of execution to ensure it can continue carrying out capital punishment.

It is unclear whether or when Tennessee could attempt to execute Pike again. Lawyers have argued it would be cruel and unusual punishment and that a new attempt could violate the prohibition on double jeopardy, trying or punishing someone twice for the same offence.

articles.title: Guernsey P&R under fire for presenting two budgets
articles.summary: Critics of P&R say it shows there is no commitment to making savings within the States.
articles.body:
Politicians have expressed dismay at Policy and Resources' (P&R) budget for 2027, stating it does not do enough to support ordinary islanders.

Deputy Adrian Gabriel said "I'm disappointed" as he hit out at plans to reduce tax caps and said he "would have liked to have seen their maximum liability, their cap, increase much more".

Deputy Haley Camp said P&R's approach of presenting two budgets showed it had abandoned all spending discipline.

P&R Treasury Lead Charles Parkinson said he never believed the direction to reduce spending by 1% in real terms - which deputies agreed to last year - was possible.

Camp disagreed: "It is clear we're only moving in one trajectory which is let's just keep on spending money with abandon and at some point down the road someone else can fix it."

Deputy Lee Van Katwyk said alongside Deputy Rob Curgenven he would be bringing a proposal to freeze fuel duty to "support struggling families".

Former head of Start Up Guernsey, Deputy Jennifer Strachan questioned P&R's plans to introduce an entrepreneurs' tax cap to attract new business to the island, alongside the States' decision to close the Digital Greenhouse, a centre for digital and creative start-ups.

"I think they're doing an easy thing, which is to say - here's a tax cap, come live here," she said.

"I think the hard work is actually developing the ecosystem for entrepreneurs to thrive."

Deputy Rob Curgenven agreed: "We've got the windfall in for pillar two and obviously GST has been agreed in principle.

"It just feels now that the cap is off and the spending spree is ready for Christmas."

Parkinson warned that simply bringing a budget with the spending cuts would lead to "a flood of amendments".

"We're only suggesting under the Option B budget half of what States committees have requested.

"We're not spending like a drunken sailor."

P&R has presented a budget which includes an inflationary increase in income tax allowances, lower taxes on a pint at the pub, a new £15m fund to encourage economic growth, £6m for initiatives to encourage States savings and the abolition of mortgage interest relief.

Deputy Aidan Matthews, who has fought to defend mortgage interest relief as previous P&R's have looked to remove it, said he would be looking to reverse this move to remove it by 2029.

He said: "I think that really the best thing that we should be doing is encouraging people to be able to afford to buy their own homes."

Alongside the Committee for Housing, P&R said it was working on initiatives to support first-time buyers.

articles.title: A mining millionaire paid $50,000 for 4,071 acres of Los Angeles land in 1882; 14 years later he gave 3,015 acres to the city, creating Griffith Park and the ground for its famous observatory
articles.summary: In 1882, mining millionaire Griffith J.
articles.body: In 1882, mining millionaire Griffith J. Griffith paid $50,000 for 4,071 acres of ranchland in the Santa Monica Mountains, a purchase that would reshape Los Angeles for generations. Fourteen years later, in 1896, he donated 3,015 acres of that land to the city, creating what is now Griffith Park and setting aside the hillside that would later hold the Griffith Observatory. The gift transformed a private cattle ranch into one of the largest urban parks in the United States, providing open space, recreation and cultural institutions for a rapidly growing city, according to the Los Angeles Department of Recreation and Parks and the Los Angeles Times.A ranch in the hills above Los AngelesThe land Griffith purchased was part of the Rancho Los Feliz, a sprawling Mexican-era grant that covered much of what is now central Los Angeles. At the time, the area was still largely rural, with oak woodlands, chaparral and grasslands covering the hills. Cattle grazed on the slopes, and the landscape bore little resemblance to the dense urban neighbourhoods that would later surround it.Griffith, a Welsh-born mining engineer who had made his fortune in Nevada silver mines, saw potential in the property beyond its immediate agricultural use. He envisioned a park that would offer city residents access to nature, fresh air and recreation at a time when Los Angeles was expanding rapidly. His purchase was an early bet on the city’s future growth and the value of preserving large tracts of open space within its boundaries.The 4,071-acre acquisition gave Griffith control of a significant portion of the eastern Santa Monica Mountains. That land included the hills that rise above the Los Feliz and Los Angeles River valleys, as well as the prominent peak that would later bear his name. By holding such a large, contiguous parcel, he positioned himself to make a gift that would be impossible to replicate once the area was subdivided and developed.The 1896 donation that created a parkIn December 1896, Griffith donated 3,015 acres of his ranch to the city of Los Angeles. The deed specified that the land be used as a public park and that it remain open and free for the people of the city. That condition helped ensure that the property would not be sold off or developed for private gain, preserving it as a permanent public resource.The donation came at a time when Los Angeles was still a relatively small city by modern standards, but one that was growing quickly. Rail lines, streetcars and new neighbourhoods were pushing outward, and civic leaders were beginning to think about parks and public spaces as essential infrastructure. Griffith’s gift provided a massive green space that could serve residents across the region for generations.Not all of Griffith’s original 4,071 acres were included in the 1896 donation. He retained some land for personal use and later development, but the 3,015-acre core became the foundation of Griffith Park. Over time, additional acquisitions and transfers would expand the park to more than 4,300 acres, making it one of the largest municipal parks in the country, as per reports.A vision for science and the starsGriffith’s plans for the park went beyond trails and picnic areas. He was fascinated by astronomy and believed that a public observatory could educate and inspire residents about science and the universe. In 1896, he wrote that he wanted to make the hills around the park a place where people could look up at the stars and learn about the heavens.That vision took decades to realise. Griffith died in 1919, but his will included a bequest to build an observatory on the land he had donated. The Griffith Observatory was constructed in the 1930s and opened to the public in 1935, perched on the southern slope of Mount Hollywood with sweeping views of the city and the Pacific. It quickly became one of Los Angeles’ most iconic landmarks.The observatory’s location within the park was no accident. Griffith had designated the hillside as an ideal site, offering elevation, visibility and accessibility. His original donation set aside that ground, so the observatory would be a part of a larger public landscape and not an isolated attraction. Today, the building and its telescopes attract millions of visitors each year and fulfilll his dream of bringing astronomy to the public, the reports say. A park for recreation and culture Today, Griffith Park has grown into a multifaceted urban resource that supports recreation, culture and conservation. It includes miles of hiking and equestrian trails, sports fields, golf courses, picnic areas and the Los Angeles Zoo. The park also houses cultural institutions such as the Autry Museum of the American West, the Greek Theatre and the Travel Town railroad museum.Those amenities reflect Griffith’s original idea of a park that would serve many purposes. He imagined a space for exercise and gathering, education and nature appreciation, all within the city’s borders. Over the years, the park has hosted everything from family picnics and school field trips to major concerts and film productions, becoming a center of Los Angeles’ civic life. The park’s size and location also make it an important ecological resource. Its hills and canyons provide habitat for native flora and fauna, including coyotes, bobcats and many species of birds. Conservation efforts within the park aim to preserve those ecosystems while allowing for public access, balancing recreation with responsibility for the environment.A complicated legacyGriffith’s gift is celebrated as one of the most important in Los Angeles history, but his legacy is also complicated. In 1897, he shot and seriously wounded his wife in a domestic violence incident, for which he was convicted and served time in San Quentin. That part of his story has prompted ongoing discussion about how cities remember donors whose personal conduct conflicts with contemporary values.Despite that history, the park and observatory continue to bear his name. City officials and historians have debated whether to rename the park or add context to its history, but as of now the Griffith name remains. The debate reflects broader questions about how to honour transformative gifts while acknowledging the flaws of the people behind them.For many Angelenos, the park itself is the most important part of the legacy. Whether or not they know the details of Griffith’s life, millions of residents benefit from the open space, trails and institutions he helped create. The park has become a shared resource that belongs to the city as much as to any individual.From ranchland to city icon The transformation of Griffith’s ranch into one of the nation’s largest urban parks is a tale of vision and civic largesse. His 1882 purchase and 1896 donation came at a time when Los Angeles was still small enough that such a gift could shape its future. As the city grew around the park, the land became increasingly valuable, both ecologically and culturally.Today, Griffith Park is a defining feature of Los Angeles, visible from freeways, neighbourhoods and the downtown skyline. The observatory, in particular, has become a symbol of the city’s relationship with science, entertainment and the night sky. Films, television shows and photographs have spread its image around the world, making it one of the most recognisable landmarks in Southern California.Griffith’s original $50,000 investment and subsequent donation created a foundation for recreation, education and conservation that continues to serve millions. “It’s a reminder that gifts of land on a grand scale can have a legacy beyond the donors, and that can shape cities in ways that are hard to predict but impossible to ignore.”You use AI every day.
