articles.title: US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
articles.summary: US Vice President Vance’s call for reduced nuclear enrichment suggests room for compromise, but major obstacles remain.
articles.body:
United States Vice President JD Vance has called for Iran to make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war, a demand experts say may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether.

His comments come amid hardline rhetoric from other senior US officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, while President Donald Trump has warned the war will end through either “the nice way or the not-so-nice way”.

Officials in Tehran, meanwhile, have questioned whether Washington genuinely wants negotiations as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month.

As both sides stake out their positions, Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that the prospect of Iran seeking a nuclear weapon has remained remote. Tehran’s negotiators are more concerned with sanctions, frozen Iranian assets, the US naval blockade and fighting across the region – issues he says remain the main obstacles to a deal.

Vance told the Reuters news agency that Iran needed to demonstrate its commitment to not developing nuclear weapons by changing its enrichment programme. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” he said.

“If you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”

Enriching uranium makes it usable as fuel for nuclear reactors or, at much higher levels, for nuclear weapons. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported that Iran had enriched uranium to 60 percent, below the roughly 90 percent considered weapons-grade. In its May 2025 assessment, it found no credible indications of a structured nuclear programme.

Vance added that the US was speaking with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, although “it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions”.

Meanwhile, Rubio, speaking to reporters in Athens, accused Iran of missing several opportunities to reach an agreement.

“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, simple, period, end of story,” he said.

He also claimed Iran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz and that its economy was “in total and complete freefall”. Under “crippling” sanctions, it was “about to reach a place few countries in the world have been”, he argued.

Analysts say the comments suggest pressure on Tehran remains central to Washington’s approach, even as Vance’s wording leaves open questions about what nuclear restrictions it would accept.

Pezeshkian said on Monday that negotiations with Washington were “futile”, accusing the US of using talks while pursuing Iran’s government.

“Our problem with the United States is that every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed upon us,” he said during a meeting with Armenia’s foreign minister.

“They have attacked us three times following talks so far; this demonstrates that they do not seek dialogue. On the contrary, their goal is to bring down the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said, according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency.

“With an enemy that resorts daily to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats – and breaks its promises – negotiations become futile, and our nation will not accept such an approach.”

However, Araghchi, addressing foreign ambassadors in Tehran on October 4, said, “Only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict, suggesting there is still room for negotiations to continue and a deal to follow.

The statements follow an Iranian proposal presented during the United Nations General Assembly in New York in late September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations. Trump subsequently rejected it.

How does this compare with previous proposals?

Iran’s latest proposal sought to build on the June 17 memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. The new proposal, offered a few weeks ago, essentially compressed the timetable and changed the sequence of steps towards a settlement.

The proposal outlined that fighting would stop on all fronts, including Israel’s offensive in Lebanon. Washington would lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets. The Strait of Hormuz would reopen after seven days, followed by negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

Experts say the proposal could have offered Trump a route to restoring shipping ahead of November’s US midterm elections. But differences over the sequence of events remain unresolved.

However, Mabon told Al Jazeera that Washington’s focus on enrichment risked overlooking Tehran’s priorities. “The US is trying to soften its stance on the nuclear question with the Iranians, but for the Iranians, this isn’t the real sticking point. It’s the blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of assets and an end to conflicts across the region.”

A deal allowing limited enrichment would also invite comparisons with the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, negotiated under US President Barack Obama. The agreement restricted Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. Trump withdrew the US from it in 2018.

Mabon said a nuclear agreement had been possible before the current war. “Arguably, a nuclear deal was within reach at several points. We had the JCPOA, of course, but then the Iranians were at the point of agreeing something similar back in February and January. The talks mediated then all suggested a nuclear agreement could be reached, and yet, the decision was taken to go to war.”

Mabon said Tehran would need commitments extending beyond the nuclear question. “I think the Iranians would require the lifting of sanctions, the lifting of the blockade and the unfreezing of assets, or at least a road map to that, alongside an end to the conflict in Lebanon and a permanent ceasefire in the Gulf.”

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains another source of uncertainty, despite Rubio’s claim that Iran has lost control of the waterway.

Although Gulf oil exports have recovered significantly, attacks on vessels continue. On Tuesday, 12 crew members on board a Panama-flagged tanker were injured by an unknown projectile while crossing the strait, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said.

Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, reached more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler. Wider Middle East crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days that month.

The recovery could ease pressure on the US to reach an agreement, although continuing attacks leave questions over how secure the passage is.

Mabon said Washington’s apparent softening on enrichment suggested it remained uncertain about how fully shipping through Hormuz had recovered.

“If the Americans were confident the strait was open properly, then they’d be pushing for a harder deal.”

articles.title: Reform internal inquiry says party did not break law over donations sting
articles.summary: Officials were recorded by undercover journalists discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.
articles.body:
An internal investigation by Reform UK has said the party did not breach electoral law when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.

Reform leader Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and the party's head of policy James Orr both stood down pending the outcome of the inquiry.

The investigation concluded that neither of the men did anything that constitutes a breach of the law.

It came after undercover filming, carried out by Verbatim Investigations and broadcast by Channel 4 News, showed the two aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

The BBC has been told Reform UK will wait until the conclusion of the police investigation before deciding the futures of Jukes and Orr.

In the Channel 4 News report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father would not be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

Elsewhere, Orr suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.

Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them. Reform says it did not commission or pay for the polls.

The party's investigation says invoices for the polling were sent to and paid for by a US company, which was set up by Verbatim.

Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.

Farage previously told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation.

Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated

Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach

Reform's investigation concluded no donation was made or accepted by the party and "the party's procedures for checking donors were never reached".

The report says Jukes commissioned the three polls personally, describing him as a "contractor" and not an employee of Reform.

It added there was "no evidence that any individual knowingly took part in an arrangement to facilitate a donation from an impermissible source".

However, it found "people speaking for the party said things that were wrong, careless and in one instance untrue".

The investigation also found "the party's arrangements allowed a sustained deception to reach its leader without anyone asking the questions that would have exposed it".

It added that the party would implement changes to "prevent that from happening again".

Jukes welcomed the findings of the investigation, saying he was "considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me".

He added: "For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities."

Reform UK said the internal investigation "found no evidence that any laws were broken".

"Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously," the party said.

"We consider that the production company - Verbatim - acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course."

A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, said: "We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself."

A Channel 4 News spokesperson said the broadcaster "stands by its journalism", adding: "The investigation underwent extensive editorial and external legal scrutiny prior to broadcast."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described the internal investigation as a "whitewash", adding: "Nothing in it exonerates Reform or Nigel Farage from the serious allegations that they still face."

articles.title: Battleground candidates clash over Trump and Cornell allegations reignite debate over campus assault: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Candidates clashed over President Donald Trump and the cost of living during debates in Maine, Georgia and Michigan.
articles.body: Candidates clashed over President Donald Trump and the cost of living during debates in Maine, Georgia and Michigan. Rape allegations at Cornell University reignite debate over campus sexual assault. And signs of the Paramount-Warner merger were visible shortly after the deal closed. Here’s what to know today. Candidates in Maine, Georgia and Michigan clash over Trump With less than a month until Election Day, candidates in the races in Maine, Georgia and Michigan boasted about their qualifications for office while trading attacks over President Donald Trump and the cost of living in a slew of Tuesday evening debates. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Democrats see the Maine race between Republican Rep. Susan Collins and her opponent, Troy Jackson, as critical to winning a Senate majority. Polls show Collins, who’s seeking a sixth term in office, in a neck-and-neck race. Jackson sought to connect Collins to Trump, name-checking the president at least 20 times in an hour and highlighted her pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Collins hit back by pitching her seniority and her role as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. She also connected Jackson’s policies to higher housing costs and property taxes in the state. Read more about the Maine debate. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson met for their lone debate in the battleground state’s gubernatorial race. Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and former Biden administration official, claimed Jackson “wants to be Trump’s favorite governor” and emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state and local taxes on things like groceries and auto insurance to combat high prices. Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, claimed Bottoms was responsible for inflation in the Atlanta area during her tenure as mayor. Read more about the Georgia debate. And in the race for Michigan governor, Democrat Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, sought to tie Republican John James to Trump’s tariff agenda and for voting against the Iran war powers resolutions. But James tried to put some daylight between himself and the president, calling for an end to the conflict. Read more about the Michigan debate. More politics news: For subscribers: Florida faces its first uncertain election in more than a decade as Democrats gain momentum in the former swing state. Here’s what leaders are saying about the races to watch. Rep. Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in Florida’s governor race, according to a new poll from NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group. A former CIA officer arrested after 600 pounds of gold bars was found stashed in his home admitted to telling a foreign official details about a secret U.S. intelligence source and lying about his background to the spy agency. A major energy industry group warned truck stops to “proceed with caution” after Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of red dye diesel fuel. America is debating campus rape. Again. Outrage exploded last week after a former Cornell University student alleged in a lawsuit that fraternity members sexually assaulted her after they coerced her to take ketamine — and that when she went to campus law enforcement for help, they did little to hold the accused men accountable. The allegations set off a cycle that has grown familiar. There are demands for change. Survivors of sexual violence share their stories. Debates stir about the definition of consent. And politicians call for new laws. When the pressure subsides, “then it falls back into the same kind of status quo, which is we’ll deal with this when it comes up,” said Jackson Katz, an author who has worked in sexual assault prevention for three decades. In the past few days, Cornell faculty members have introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the school administration’s handling of the case. Student protesters have called for Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff’s resignation. And Sally Yates, a longtime federal prosecutor who has clashed with President Trump, will lead an independent review of how the university responds to misconduct on campus. This time, experts and advocates hope there’s lasting change. How the debate has evolved over the last four decades. Paramount-Warner merger marks a new era in entertainment There’s a new mega studio in town and signs of change were clear almost immediately. On the famous Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank, California, “A Skydance Corporation” was added below the iconic logo. Similar branding was seen at the company’s New York City office. Early Tuesday, Paramount Skydance completed the $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, handing CEO David Ellison control of one of the world’s largest entertainment companies. The new branding is a sign that Ellison isn’t taking any time to dwell on the past. The merger comes at a moment of significant change in Hollywood and will likely come with consequences that could affect the entire industry. How the deal came together and what could happen next. Israelis abroad told to exercise ‘heightened vigilance’ on Oct. 7 anniversary Three years after Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage in the Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are marking the anniversary of an event that traumatized the nation and reshaped the region. Memorials have been held at homes, roadsides, kibbutzim and the Nova music festival site, where militants killed more than 360 people and took 44 hostages. Israel’s National Security Council has warned Israelis living abroad to exercise “heightened vigilance” amid an “increased risk of attempted attacks against Israelis and Jews abroad,” on the anniversary. In a statement issued by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, the public was urged to “refrain from posting details about travel plans abroad on social media in advance” as well as “posting content on social media that indicates service in the security forces.” Follow our live coverage of the anniversary. Staff Pick: 7 million fewer working women get paid time off than men Gender equality in the workplace is not limited to how much men and women are paid, it also includes the benefits they receive. When the Bureau of Labor Statistics released a survey last month asking Americans about their access to paid leave, I was intrigued by what the numbers said. It had been seven years since the BLS had last asked the same question, so I was surprised to see that while overall access had increased, a gap persisted between men and women. So I talked with experts who study work and family about the trend, and they weren’t surprised. Women work part-time or flexible roles at higher rates than men do, often to accommodate caregiving responsibilities at home, these experts told me. I learned this can create a reinforcing cycle: Women are in these roles so they can care for family, and in turn, are unable to advance to jobs which would provide the benefit. — Joelle Gross, data reporter NBC Selected: Last chance to save big during Prime Day And just like that, Prime Day is almost over. You can still save big; many retailers are having sales this week, and these are the best ones we’ve seen at Best Buy, Target and more. articles.title: KARL ROVE: Fox News changed the media 30 years ago. The best is yet to come
articles.summary: Thirty years ago this week, along came Fox News. On the news side, it aimed for fairness and balance in its coverage. And Fox News hosts have won respect.
articles.body: Thirty years ago, on Oct. 7, 2026, Fox News burst on the scene. It arrived just in time. Journalism as practiced in print, television and cable had become, on the national level, infected by subtle bias. Important stories went unreported because they didn’t fit into the mindset of a largely insular community. This community dominated the major national channels. It consisted of executives, producers, anchors, reporters, writers and researchers. The closer these individuals were to the top of their networks, the more they tended to come from the same universities, live in the same towns and socialize with each other. They tended to share liberal or left-of-center attitudes and biases that permeated their choice of stories and the nature of their coverage. They were mostly unaware of this bias. If they were aware, some didn’t care. They were in a position to set the agenda and shape the storyline and were happy to do so. Then along came Fox News. On the news side, it aimed for fairness and balance. Its anchors and on-air personalities strove to cover issues and events that were important to the audience and the country, not just what advanced someone’s bias. Like most Americans, the news side of Fox consists of people who love our country, see her greatness as well as her challenges and connect with people all across the nation who want fairness and balance. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE Over the years, these Fox News figures have won the respect of both competitors and the nation’s newsmakers. They’ve interviewed leaders of our country and the world. Fox anchors have been on the stage asking questions in presidential primary and general election debates involving both parties. Fox Sunday morning programs, both on the channel and on Fox Business, have become must-do stops for newsmakers and must-watch television for Americans who want to learn what is actually going on. In all these settings, Fox News on-air personalities have raised important issues other networks ignored or downplayed. They’ve developed reputations as hard-working journalists who do their homework, know the facts and ask tough, fair questions of all who sit before their cameras. JENNIFER GRIFFIN: I COVERED WARS, TERROR AND TRAGEDY FOR FOX NEWS. WHAT I FOUND WAS A FAMILY On the opinion side of Fox, the on-air personalities are conservative, patriotic and proud of our country. They’re passionate about sharing their views. And as they strive for a respectful national conversation, they’re confident enough to share their studios with figures to the left of center. That is why, for example, "The Five," originally an experiment to fill space while programming was rejiggered, has turned out to be such a popular and durable part of the Fox lineup. Imagine — people from the left and right talking about issues, often disagreeing and sometimes agreeing, but always doing so with empathy, intelligence, wit and, oh, yes, good humor! MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME This combination of fair and balanced news coverage and an opinion voice for a large element of the country that was ignored — and, in some cases, looked down upon by those who ran the existing national media — has made for an exciting three decades for Fox. This network has become a vital part of America’s national dialogue, and I’ve been honored to be part of it since January 2008. What an exciting time lies ahead as the channel’s leadership encourages even greater efforts toward fair and balanced coverage of the big events affecting our country and the world. articles.title: German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
articles.summary: Former top spy August Hanning led the Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.
articles.body:
The man who led Germany’s intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005 has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason, according to the country’s federal prosecutor’s office.

The office announced on Tuesday that August Hanning, 80, was arrested and faces charges including “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services.

The office has not specified which country or countries Hanning is accused of working for.

Citing unnamed sources, however, German news outlet Der Spiegel reported that Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijan intelligence agency representative. In 2025, prosecutors also accused Hanning of ties with Israeli spies in a separate case which ultimately led them to the ex-intelligence boss’s alleged espionage for other agencies.

If found guilty, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in Germany.

German news outlet Deutsche Welle described Hanning’s arrest as Germany’s “biggest espionage scandal of the century”.

Born in Nordwalde, Westphalia, western Germany, in 1946, Hanning served as the head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and later moved to work in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, before working as a state secretary until 2009.

He later worked as a private consultant.

German media showed pictures of Hanning being taken from his red-brick house in Norwalde, close to Munster, to a bulletproof vehicle by masked officers on Tuesday morning.

They claim Hanning used classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for a foreign intelligence service and kept “close contact” with another foreign spying service for “several years” while he was working as a private consultant.

They say that in 2010, Hanning came to an agreement to receive confidential information from his former bureau chief – who was in office until March this year and is named only as “Manfred D” – and was preparing to provide an “analysis” of it to a foreign power in exchange for money. It is unclear if the analysis was duly shared.

However, Hanning is also alleged to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, partly based on information provided by Manfred D, to a contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.

Manfred D was also arrested on Tuesday and charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

“Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” a statement from the prosecutor’s office said.

Over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, “many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings”, it added.

“Hanning was to capitalise on said information in the context of his private consulting services, which he had since been offering,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The alleged espionage by Hanning and Manfred D was uncovered during an investigation into a separate kidnapping case involving German businesswoman and steakhouse chain heiress, Christina Block.

In that case, Hamburg prosecutors accused Block of arranging the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Prosecutors said Hanning put Block in touch with a private Israeli espionage firm to carry out the abductions. The former spy chief and a police officer were accused of accepting more than 100,000 euros ($112,000) from Block in exchange for returning her children from Denmark, where they were living with her ex-husband. The trial is ongoing.

What do we know about the alleged documents that were passed on?

Little detail is available about the contents of the 2,000 documents, but German news outlet Suddeutsche Zeitung reported that a number of them related to Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military.

It added that other materials were highly sensitive and classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries.

Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to the AFP news agency that Berlin would not “tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.

“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he said, adding that Hanning’s alleged actions would amount to “trampling his official duties underfoot”.

The current head of the BND, Martin Jaeger, told the German Rheinische Post newspaper that the agency had “quickly carried out extensive internal investigations” into the former chief before federal prosecutors took over the case.

“For the BND and for me, there are no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jaeger said, adding that it had “not called into question any of my aims or any of my priorities”.

Have there been similar spy scandals in Germany before?

In 2023, a high-ranking German intelligence officer, identified as “Carsten L”, was charged with high treason when prosecutors alleged he had obtained classified intelligence on the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and shared it with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). His case is ongoing.

In 1974, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign following revelations that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms, forecast to become a hurricane and hit the Gulf Coast this week
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Isaias formed early Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before hitting the U.S.
articles.body: MIAMI — Tropical Storm Isaias formed early Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before hitting the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week. Isaias was located about 285 miles (460 kilometers) west of Progreso, Mexico, and about 580 miles (935 kilometers) southwest of the Mississippi River’s mouth, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. It had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph (13 kph). It was not immediately known where the storm may make landfall on the Gulf Coast. The hurricane center’s initial projections said the center of Isaias could come onshore somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the western Florida Panhandle. People in those areas were urged to prepare for the storm. “There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast,” the hurricane center said. “Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place.” Isaias will also bring areas of heavy rain to portions of the Gulf Coast and much of the U.S. Southeast on Friday and into the weekend, forecasters said. The storm comes as the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year due to a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. articles.title: Yorkshire Water's £1.5m sewage reduction scheme in Ripon falls short
articles.summary: The firm says the scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges has not performed as expected.
articles.body:
Yorkshire Water has admitted a £1.5m scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges into a North Yorkshire river has not performed as expected.

When the investment was announced in 2024 for the River Ure in Ripon, the water company said the scheme would reduce the issue by about 75%.

But it said the number of recorded discharges from its Clock Tower combined sewer overflow (CSO), near the Ripon by-pass bridge, fell from 75 in 2021 to 43 in 2025, a reduction of about 43%.

The company has described the result as "disappointing", but stressed that comparing individual years was complicated by rainfall levels.

"[2025] was a particularly dry year, which will have further contributed to a decrease in discharges," a Yorkshire Water spokesperson said.

"As such, whilst there has been a reduction, the scheme did not perform as expected, which is disappointing."

Combined sewer overflows are designed as pressure-relief points on sewer networks which carry both wastewater and rainwater.

During heavy rainfall, they can discharge into watercourses to prevent overloaded sewers backing up into homes, businesses and streets.

Such discharges can be permitted by the Environment Agency under specified circumstances.

Recent testing by campaign group Stop Ure Pollution and the Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust further upstream has raised concerns about bacteria and other pollution in the river, the Local Democracy Service reports .

The Skipton and Ripon branch of the North Yorkshire Green Party has now submitted an Environmental Information Regulations request, seeking information held by Yorkshire Water about the performance of the Clock Tower scheme and changes in discharges following work carried out in 2025.

Green Party councillor Andy Brown said the levels of sewage going in the rivers "is deeply disgusting" and called the latest testing further upstream "far from reassuring".

He said campaigners and organisations, including Ripon City Council, would continue pressing for improvements.

"Yorkshire Water must play its part," he said.

"It must act, and it must deliver the facts – straight-up and undiluted."

Yorkshire Water said it was investigating further projects in Ripon as part of a £1.5bn investment programme aimed at reducing storm overflow use.

"We know there is much more to do to protect local watercourses," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Yes, Zionism is racism
articles.summary: And there is nothing radical about declaring it. It is a fact of history.
articles.body:
On Sunday, at its annual conference in Brighton, the British Green Party voted to recognise Zionism as racism. The motion, which describes Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project”, passed with 1,022 votes to 813, despite opposition from several of the party’s MPs as well as former party leader Caroline Lucas .

The vote caused uproar in the British mainstream, with many commentators taking to the airwaves and social media to condemn it, accuse the party of anti-Semitism and even claim it is endangering Jewish people.

Yet, the Green Party’s resolution does not declare anything radical or extraordinary. Zionism was and continues to be a settler-colonial ideology, and settler colonialism is fundamentally racist. Zionism is centred on the belief that Jewish people from anywhere in the world have a right to a homeland in historic Palestine – a right that outweighs any other people’s.

It is a conviction that is based on biblical claims to a land and an ahistorical understanding of history. Crucially, its fulfilment requires the usurping and dispossession of the indigenous Palestinian population.

It should not be particularly controversial to define Zionism as a settler colonial ideology, particularly as the Zionist founding fathers themselves proudly described it as such. Vladimir Jabotinsky, a leading Revisionist Zionist thinker of the early 20th century, wrote that “Zionist colonization … must be carried out in defiance of the will of the native population”.

Theodor Herzl, often cited as the founding father of political Zionism, hoped to establish contact with Cecil Rhodes, the imperialist who led British colonisation in Zimbabwe.

In an infamous draft letter, which Herzl never sent, he invited Rhodes to “help make history”. “It doesn’t involve Africa but a piece of Asia Minor … How then, do I happen to turn to you since this is an out the way matter for you? … Because it is something colonial,” he wrote.

Zionism’s early institutions also reflected the same colonial self-identification through their names: the Jewish Colonial Trust, the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, the Jewish Agency’s Colonization Department.

Zionism is also not particularly exceptional as an ideology. It follows the path of other ideologies often rooted in the idea of manifest destiny that have shaped settler-colonial entities and their genocidal crimes committed against indigenous populations to secure the continuation of their colonial projects.

Indeed, what is unfolding in Palestine is not an isolated event but part of a global history of violent, dispossessive tactics aimed at eliminating indigenous peoples and solidifying settler-colonial control over land.

The Green Party was not the first to define Zionism as racism in an official position. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 3379 declaring Zionism as a form of racism and racial discrimination. The resolution passed by 72 votes to 35 with 32 abstentions and drew on statements by the Organisation of African Unity and the Non-Aligned Movement made earlier that year.

It is not surprising that the resolution was championed by Global South countries who knew all too well the workings of colonial ideologies. Many rightly drew comparisons between the Zionist regime and South Africa’s apartheid regime.

The resolution was eventually repealed in 1991 under pressure from the United States and with the approval of the Soviet Union. The Israeli regime had made its revocation a condition for attending the Madrid peace talks, cosponsored by Washington and Moscow. The resolution’s repeal reflected a shift in the balance of geopolitical power, against the backdrop of the Soviet Union’s dissolution and the collapse of the Eastern bloc, rather than a reconsideration of the global understanding of Zionism.

The fact that a British mainstream party has returned to something put forward by Global South countries on the world stage five decades earlier is significant. In the British political and historical context, it is a small but important step towards confronting the country’s dark legacy of facilitating the creation of a Zionist state on Palestinian land and contributing to the Nakba, the 1948 ethnic cleansing of Palestine.

Whether the Green Party will be able to hold its position under the immense pressure it is sure to face and avoid making concessions to appease those who attack it is yet to be seen.

Meanwhile, as this all plays out in the Western media, the genocide in Palestine continues, and what has been lost in the noise is the material reality of Zionism for Palestinians on the ground. For more than a century, this ideology has created untold devastation and destruction for the Palestinian people. The Green Party motion did not invent this history – it merely named it.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Palestinian killed, 16 wounded in Israeli pogrom in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: A 44-year-old Palestinian man was killed during Israeli settler assaults on olive harvesters in the West Bank.
articles.body:
A Palestinian has been killed and 16 others wounded in a pogrom by settlers under the protection of Israeli forces in the northern occupied West Bank, Palestinian authorities said.

Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, from Burqa, northwest of Nablus, was killed in the attack on Palestinians harvesting olives on farmland near Burqa, west of Nablus, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.

Several of those wounded, including a woman, were taken to hospitals in Tulkarem and Nablus, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported, citing local sources.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) said its teams treated five people in the area, including two who suffered gunshot wounds, while the other three were beaten, Wafa reported.

PRCS said Israeli forces also assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the injured people, and briefly detained three paramedics and a volunteer.

Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah, said the violence comes amid escalating attacks on Palestinians during the olive harvest season.

“If you just go to pick your olives now … you could not return from the journey. It could be dangerous, not only because of Israeli restrictions against farmers going to their lands, but also because of the armed Israeli settlers who continue to assault Palestinians,” Ibrahim said.

She said the attacks have transformed an important social and economic season for Palestinian families.

“In October, usually Palestinians take days off from their jobs and go to the land, try and pick their olives because this is supposed to be a joyous season,” she added.

Israeli forces and settlers also assaulted several Palestinians harvesting olives near Anata in the central occupied West Bank, Wafa reported.

Elsewhere, settlers cut down at least 50 olive trees belonging to the Palestinian Siam family after attacking the village of Mikhmas, northeast of occupied East Jerusalem.

Ibrahim said attacks have affected olive farming, with at least 45,000 trees destroyed across the occupied West Bank this year.

Since October 7, 2023 there have been almost 15,000 settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, with 66 Palestinians killed, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.

One such pogrom, backed by Israeli forces in the village of Marda, north of Salfit, injured a number of Palestinians picking olives on Wednesday. They were treated for tear gas inhalation by the PRCS, according to Wafa, which says Israeli forces detained at least three Palestinians.

Separately, a Palestinian was injured after being shot with live ammunition by Israeli forces during a raid near the al-Aqsa restaurant in Jenin. The injured man was taken to hospital by PRCS.

Israeli forces detained a Palestinian and imposed a curfew on residents in Burqa, as settlers raided the village east of Ramallah.

articles.title: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win Nobel chemistry prize for ‘mirror image’ work
articles.summary: Scientists honoured for solving mystery of asymmetric molecules that has helped in manufacture of pharmaceuticals.
articles.body:
Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a longstanding riddle of asymmetric “mirror image” molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Wednesday the pair – Kagan, 95, from France; and Soai, 76, from Japan – were honoured “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.

Their findings showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favour a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.

Many of the molecules essential to life exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands. Yet living organisms almost exclusively use only one version, a phenomenon known as “homochirality” – from the Greek word for hand – that has puzzled chemists for more than a century.

“The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need methods for selectively preparing them,” said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.

“In developing such methods, the findings of this year’s laureates are important. They provided powerful tools for that,” he said.

Heiner Linke, chair of the committee, said the two scientists provided “a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously”, calling the chemical reactions they developed “spectacular”.

Soai, speaking by phone to the Nobel Prize news conference, said he had been out shopping when he received the news.

“This is the most exciting day in my life, I am very glad to share this prize with Professor Henri Kagan,” he added.

Last year’s chemistry award went to scientists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for the development of so-called metal-organic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of freshwater.

The chemistry Nobel is always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, following those for medicine and physics .

The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, while the keenly anticipated peace prize is due on Friday.

Established in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars.

Nobel, a chemist by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank.

articles.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
articles.summary: The sale of the High Street chain was announced on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.

Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy 177-year-old company on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.

Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.

The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.

Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.

It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.

In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.

Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".

She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.

The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.

Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".

Boots gets new US owner in multi-billion dollar deal

The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.

It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business.

As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic.

It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since.

Weston, who will become chairman of Boots, signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.

"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.

The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.

The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.

The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.

The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn.

Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.

Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

articles.title: Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers
articles.summary: There have been many cases of top spies giving classified information to enemy nations. Here are some of the highlights.
articles.body:
Germany’s former spy chief, August Hanning, has been arrested on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service.

Hanning, 80, headed up the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005.

A federal prosecutor’s statement said it strongly suspected him of “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services since 2010, while working as a private consultant. He is accused of obtaining around 2,000 sensitive documents from a former bureau chief who has also been arrested.

But he isn’t the only high-ranking intelligence officer to have been discovered to have worked for foreign governments over the years.

1940s to 1960s – Kim Philby and the ‘Cambridge Five’

Kim Philby was a British intelligence officer who secretly spent decades working for the Soviet Union during World War II and the early Cold War years.

He was recruited by Soviet Intelligence while studying at Cambridge University in the 1930s. He was the most prominent member of the “Cambridge Five” – a spy ring that gave away British secrets to the Soviet Union.

During the war, he joined MI6, where he rose to head its counter-Soviet division, and was later posted to Washington, DC. This gave him access to sensitive information through his close links to the CIA and FBI.

His tip-offs to his Soviet handlers are believed to have scuppered many Western operations and revealed the identities of agents. This included information operations to overthrow Albania’s communist leader Enver Hoxha as part of Western efforts to stop the spread of communism.

Philby came under suspicion in 1951 and was forced out of MI6 when Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean, two other members of the Cambridge Five, defected to the Soviet Union. Philby was suspected of having warned them that British intelligence officers were close to uncovering their identities as double agents for the Soviet Union, before being formally cleared of the allegations in 1955.

Then, in 1963, aware that the net was closing in on him because of his own involvement with Soviet intelligence, he fled to Russia, where he lived with his wife since 1971, Rufina Pukhova, until his death in 1988. Overall, he provided state secrets, the identities of agents, minutes from cabinet meetings, atomic research, diplomatic and military intelligence, and information about counter-intelligence operations to the Soviet Union for nearly 20 years.

Philby is regarded as the most damaging spy in British history.

According to the UK’s National Archives, one of the agents he unmasked to the Soviet Union was Constantin Volkov, a Soviet intelligence officer posted to Turkiye who wanted to defect to the UK in 1945. Volkov and his wife were seized and executed in Moscow as a result. The information he provided to the Soviet Union about a joint CIA-MI6 operation in communist Albania in the late 1940s and early 1950s resulted in the execution of hundreds of anti-communist agents.

Oleg Gordievsky was a KGB colonel who spied for British intelligence for more than a decade.

He was the son of an officer in the NKVD, which was the Soviet secret police and the direct predecessor to the KGB.

But he was recruited by MI6 in the early 1970s after becoming disillusioned by the Soviet crushing of mass protests during the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia in 1968 and the building of the Berlin Wall.

While working for the KGB, he was stationed in Copenhagen and later in London, where he became KGB station chief in 1985.

The intelligence he provided to the British is thought to have revealed the KGB’s deep concerns that NATO’s 1983 Able Archer exercise might be cover for a real nuclear strike. This was invaluable for helping the West understand Soviet fears and to de-escalate.

Gordievsky came under suspicion and was recalled to Moscow in 1985. He was drugged and interrogated but had not yet been charged when MI6 ran a daring operation to rescue him and smuggle him out of Russia in the boot of a car across the Finnish border.

Russia sentenced Gordievsky to death in absentia.

He lived in the UK under protection until his death in 2025.

Robert Hanssen was a high-ranking agent at the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) who spied for the Soviet Union and later for Russian intelligence services between 1979 and 2001.

Hanssen initially studied dentistry at Northwestern University before switching courses and receiving a degree in accounting and information systems. He worked as a police officer in Chicago before joining the FBI in 1976.

He approached Soviet military intelligence in 1979, eventually working with the KGB and its successor, the SVR. He operated using the alias “Ramon Garcia”.

Hanssen never met his handlers in person, instead using “dead drops” when he would leave classified documents in prearranged outdoor locations, including parks, wooded areas, under bridges and on street corners in the Washington, DC area, in exchange for cash or diamonds.

He handed over thousands of pages of classified material, including details about US nuclear war plans and the identities of Russian officials working for the US. At least two of those sources, including Dmitri Polyakov and Valery Marynov were executed.

The arrest in 1994 of Aldrich Ames, another US spy caught working for Russian intelligence, eventually led to his arrest in February 2001.

He pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty and died in prison in 2023.

Alexander Yuk Ching Ma is a former CIA officer who was caught spying for China.

He worked for the CIA from 1982 to 1989 and became a US citizen, living in Honolulu.

In March 2001, officers of China’s Shanghai State Security Bureau asked him to arrange a meeting with a now-deceased former CIA officer who served from 1967 to 1983. The two met in a Hong Kong hotel room for three days. In exchange for $50,000, they provided classified information to China.

The FBI became aware of his ties to Chinese intelligence and hired him as a contract linguist in its Honolulu office so that his activities could be monitored.

He was arrested in a sting after admitting to an undercover FBI employee that he had facilitated the provision of classified information to Chinese intelligence.

Ma pleaded guilty in May 2024 and is currently serving a 10-year prison sentence.

articles.title: Tanker attacks in Strait of Hormuz highest in a week since Iran war began: Report
articles.summary: Attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz last week were reportedly the most frequent of any week since the Iran war began.
articles.body: Attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz last week were reportedly the most frequent of any week since the Iran war began.According to maritime security sources tracking incidents in the area, the surge comes as Gulf producers step up their exports. Reuters reported.In the week of September 28 to October 5, there were at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait, according to data from three maritime security sources, cited by the Reuters news agency.The sources said this was the highest weekly total since the US war with Iran started on 28 February.The International Maritime Organisation (IMO), the UN's shipping agency, reported separate data showing nine incidents involving vessels in the same week. articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities kill at least 21 in a major attack that Kyiv saw coming
articles.summary: Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 21 civilians, including four children, and wounding around 60 in Moscow’s latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 21 civilians, including four children, and wounding around 60 in Moscow’s latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said. Ukraine had anticipated the attack, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning the previous day that intelligence services had concluded that Russia was building up for a “massive” strike. Although Ukraine knew about the looming attack, which coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday, it couldn’t fend it off completely. The deaths and damage illustrated the difficulty Ukraine has in countering Russia’s ballistic missiles and the new jet-powered drones used in Moscow’s escalating bombardments. Without ammunition for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukraine can’t stop Russian ballistic weapons. It is racing to develop a new generation of interceptors fast enough to catch Moscow’s high-flying jet-propelled drones. Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a long-range aerial war as their armies remain largely deadlocked on the battlefield, more than 4 ½ years after Moscow’s all-out invasion of its neighbor. The unrelenting aerial attacks are hurting Russia but could be ruinous for smaller Ukraine. U.S.-led peace efforts appear unlikely to bring any short-term relief, with the possibility of holding low-level technical talks still under discussion. Putin, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with the invasion in the belief that Ukrainians will buckle under the pressure and Kyiv’s Western supporters won’t stay the course, Western analysts say. “Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. “Trying to make daily life impossible for Ukrainians who want to live in peace.” Russia wants Ukrainians to be afraid to fall asleep, official says A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, killing 15 people, including four children, and wounding about 50, authorities said. Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including the capital Kyiv, according to Zelenskyy. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media. Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war. “Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskyy said. In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the regional military administration, and a rescue operation was continuing. “That is exactly what the enemy is counting on. For us to be afraid to fall asleep. To let our children out of our sight. To plan anything. So that everyone thinks: next time it could be my address,” he said. Russia’s Defense Ministry said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine. The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit. Ukraine strikes back with attacks on Russian oil facilities, Zelenskyy says Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles at oil refineries and storage depots. Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions of Russia. Russian officials made no immediate comment. Zelenskyy also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi. It was not possible to independently verify the images. Some Russian online media late Tuesday also posted the images. Unconfirmed media reports said it was carrying oil from Novorossiysk to India and was attacked by Ukrainian sea drones.

articles.title: Nickelodeon parent guides tackle gender identity, anti-racism and Islamophobia
articles.summary: Nickelodeon's parent resources page offers guides on gender identity, anti-racism, and countering Islamophobia, drawing sharp criticism online.
articles.body: The popular children’s network Nickelodeon is facing criticism over its "Parent Resources" webpage, which provides guides for discussing anti-racism, gender identity, and other social issues with children. The resources touch upon various controversial topics, such as "countering Islamophobia" and "How to talk to kids about the attack on the Capitol," while providing talking points for parents and caregivers on how to approach each subject with their children, according to the website. In one 31-page document, Nickelodeon — in partnership with the LGBT organization Glisten, formerly known as GLSEN — lays out a step-by-step guide for teachers titled "Talk & Take Action: An Educators' Guide to Combating LGBTQIA+ Discrimination." "When preparing to talk about topics around identity, gender, and sexuality with students, it’s important to frame those discussions in ways that maximize opportunities to learn, while at the same time ensuring that students don’t leave the encounter confused, afraid, or traumatized," the guide reads. PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT "This guide delves into misgendering, discriminatory acts, and other forms of discrimination the LGBTQ+ community has endured, which can be challenging for all of us to read and talk about," it continues. The guide goes on to provide educators with a glossary of terms relating to the LGBTQ community and tips on how to "foster an inclusive classroom" for students — such as displaying LGBTQ flags and posters in their classrooms. Another resource titled "Talk and Take Action: Parents', Caregivers' and Educators' Guide to Countering Islamophobia" lays out the "history of activism against Islamophobia," while also providing parents with a discussion guide on educating children about the Muslim faith. "Explore the basic tenets of Islam. Similar to Judaism and Christianity, people who practice Islam believe in one God, called Allah," the guide states. The guide goes on to provide talking points for young children regarding how they can speak up if they encounter an individual who is being bullied for their faith, while encouraging the reader to be an "Upstander" for their peers. HARVARD OFFERS ‘ANTI-RACIST’ RESOURCES FOR PARENTS AS STUDENTS HEAD BACK TO SCHOOL It then lists examples of ways a child could respond if they encounter someone who is being bullied because of their Islamic faith, such as saying, "Hey, that is mean. Remember, your words can hurt people." Another Nickelodeon document, "Talking to Kids: Capitol Attack Resources," provides links for adults discussing the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021, with children. The webpage and its resources have drawn criticism from social media users and a psychotherapist who told Fox News Digital that the guides go beyond the network's traditional entertainment role. In a reply to Libs of TikTok’s X post sharing the guides, one user wrote, "Kids network with a parent guide on gender and anti-racism. That’s not cartoons and that’s NOT fun. That’s recruitment. Keep them off it." MS RACHEL DEFENDS HER ACTIVISM BY POINTING TO MISTER ROGERS' POLITICAL LEGACY ON CHILDREN'S TV HOW MS RACHEL'S POLITICAL ACTIVISM IS SPARKING PUSHBACK FROM PARENTS Another user blasted the content, writing on X, "A kids’ network pushing ‘anti-racism,’ gender ideology, and the rest to parents as official resources. They’re not hiding it anymore. Parents, check what your kids’ shows are linking." Jonathan Alpert, a New York-based psychotherapist and author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital the guides could force children to begin looking at the world from a political lens prematurely, therefore harming their ability to relate to their peers. "There’s nothing controversial about teaching kids not to bully someone because of their religion. That’s basic decency and every parent should support and get behind that," Alpert told Fox News Digital. "But once you start teaching 7-year-olds about systemic discrimination and white supremacy, you’ve crossed into something very different." Alpert added that young children are not focused on "weighing different ideas about race and society," adding that "kids absorb what an adult in authority tells them is true." According to Alpert, the network’s encouragement of parents and educators discussing controversial — and often political — topics could have an unintended negative impact on the children they are teaching. "At an age when they should be learning how to get along with each other, adults are introducing complex ideas about power, privilege and oppression," Alpert said. "This may actually be teaching kids to focus on differences they otherwise wouldn’t be thinking much about." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Nickelodeon declined a request by Fox News Digital for comment.

articles.title: ‘Bar Fairies,’ a Community Activist Group, Fight Drunk Driving With Free Coffee
articles.summary: “Bar Fairies,” the community activist group that gives out coffee to drivers who leave their cars at the bar, was founded in Montana to fight drunk driving.
articles.body: “It was really important to me as a mom that my son did not die in vain,” says Beth McBride. Every weekend, McBride and her daughter, Carli Seymour, search the Flathead Valley for vehicles left overnight in bar parking lots. When they find one, they leave the driver a note and $5 coffee gift card. “I didn’t want him to just be another statistic of somebody killed by a drunk driver,” she adds. In March 2023, a repeat drunk driver killed McBride’s son, Bobby Dewbre, on his 21st birthday, while he was out celebrating with friends. He was crossing the street to get a sober ride home. The note contains a photo of Dewbre and tells the recipient how he died. Montana has one of the highest rates of DUI fatalities in the U.S. “Bobby was an incredible young man,” McBride tells TODAY.com, remembering him as “super positive” and “fun to be around.” According to data from the Montana Department of Public Health & Human Services, 19.5% of Montana adults report binge drinking at least once in the last month, over 4% higher than the national average. Alcohol-related deaths among Montanans have been on the rise: There were 1,563 between 2009 and 2013, and 2,941 between 2019 and 2023. “It sucks he can’t be here and that Bobby doesn’t get to be an adult,” Seymour tells TODAY.com. “When I think about where he would be right now, it stops me in my tracks. It freaking sucks so bad.” “You can always kind of see these things happen to other people and picture how you might feel, but it is so enveloping,” she continues. “It’s the only it’s the only thing that you can think about. The only thing that you can do is be devastated.” Early one morning, Seymour says she was driving to her mom’s home and spotted something different about a bar she passed. “I noticed that there was a bar that had a lot of cars left overnight, and it was March, so it was cold in the morning,” she says, describing the frost on the car windows. “I could tell that they had been left from the night before. I just wanted to tell them thank you somehow.” Seymour says Montanans are used to driving on long roads, “steeped in a drinking-and-driving culture.” “You watch the adults in your life drink and drive,” she adds. Seymour was working as a barista at a local coffee shop when her brother died. She asked what they could do to thank drivers who decided not to drive drunk. The coffee boost idea came naturally. Sampson remembers the daughter of a former coworker: A drunk driver crashed his drunk into the bedroom of 15-year-old Erin Howk and killed her while she was asleep. “That’s the culture that I grew up in. That’s the culture that other Montanans and other rural Americans have grown up in,” she continues. “It is inconvenient. It is a change from your normal routine, and so we wanted to give just a little sweetness to make that feel a little better.” The idea is spreading: McBride says the 30-square-mile Flathead Valley currently has 75 volunteers and, as of today, 309 people have signed up. They say Fairies are getting their wings across the U.S. — in Salem, Oregon; Las Vegas, Nevada; Hattiesburg, Mississippi; Houston, Lansdale, Pennsylvania; Bucks County, Pennsylvania; Washington, D.C.; and Cleveland, Ohio. “We have been told by people who have received cards over and over and over again that that card made them think,” McBride says, adding that multiple people have pledged to the organization that they’ll no longer drink and drive. In 2025, the Montana Legislature passed House Bill 267, also known as “Bobby’s Law,” which strengthens the punishment for DUIs that result in death. Seymour says, if rewarding a driver’s decision to find another way home prevents one more death, it’s worth it. “I don’t want to absolve anybody of the responsibility for their own actions, but I do think it’s really important to kind of take a recovery standpoint from it,” she says. “Tomorrow’s a new day. We can all become better over time.”

articles.title: More than 200,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen, UN says
articles.summary: With 3,700 fleeing to Djibouti amid Houthi clashes, the UN warns three in four families in parts of Yemen face hunger.
articles.body:
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to data released by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The IOM described the crisis in a statement on Wednesday as alarming, with displacement figures surging from 76,000 in mid-September to more than 200,000.

“People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope, calling for increased funding amid soaring needs for food and shelter.

Yemen is experiencing its most serious escalation in fighting since a UN-brokered truce largely halted major cross-border attacks in 2022.

The Iran-backed Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, seized the country’s entire Red Sea coast last month from Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government based in the southern port of Aden.

On Sunday, Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced an offensive to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the armed group has controlled since 2014.

Displacements have been recorded across Yemen, with the southwestern governorate of Taiz taking the heaviest blow.

More than 3,700 people have also fled by sea to Djibouti , the IOM said.

On Friday, the UN World Food Programme warned that three in four families in parts of Yemen were going hungry due to the “absolutely devastating” impact of the renewed conflict.

articles.title: Lawyers seek to block Texas man’s execution, citing failed execution of Christa Pike
articles.summary: Lawyers for a Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk are asking a judge to stay his execution by lethal injection set for Wednesday, citing the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
articles.body: DALLAS — Lawyers for a Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk are asking a judge to stay his execution by lethal injection set for Wednesday, citing the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week. This would be the first execution scheduled in the U.S. since Pike. Because the same drug used in her attempted execution — pentobarbital — would be used in Texas for Jamaal Howard, his attorneys argued that the drug poses the same risks, and said they believe the state’s supply had become degraded. Pike’s lawyers are seeking more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old survived two doses of pentobarbital. She was hospitalized and, as of Tuesday, was awake and speaking. Her attorneys have alleged her execution was marred by blown veins, where a needle goes all the way through a vein and causes a leak of blood and fluid, as well as Tennessee’s deteriorated pentobarbital and a lack of emergency medical care. “There is a similar risk,” Howard’s attorneys wrote, “that Texas’s execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind.” Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard, which would be the 30th execution nationwide in 2026. A killing caught on surveillance video Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery. Evidence presented at the trial included the store’s surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout. Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles (161 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records. His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said that he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability. He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities. Motion to stay because of drugs The motion filed in the Court of Criminal Appeals in Texas early Wednesday said Howard’s attorneys had filed requests for information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use. They say the department asked for a state attorney general opinion about whether they would have to disclose that information, despite a “years-long practice of disclosing information.” The Texas attorney general opinion is not expected to be returned until after Wednesday, meaning Howard can’t litigate whatever decision the state might make on releasing that information, they say. Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday morning. Executions in the US this year Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method. Tennessee’s Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.

articles.title: KSE confirms plans to rejoin BJP, eyes 2028 assembly polls
articles.summary: Karnataka’s KS Eshwarappa says talks are underway to rejoin BJP and confirms plans to contest the 2028 assembly polls, with son Kantesh also considered.
articles.body: Shivamogga: Former deputy chief minister and Rashtrabhaktara Balaga convener KS Eshwarappa on Wednesday said that consultations regarding his formal re-entry into BJP remain ongoing, while affirming his plan to contest the assembly elections in 2028.Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the politician said discussions are on with organisational leaders from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, community heads and political supporters. He noted that well-wishers have urged him to secure clear assurances prior to rejoining the saffron party to avoid a repeat of past ticket denials. Eshwarappa was denied a ticket in the 2023 assembly polls, which led to his expulsion from the party as he rebelled against the party in the Lok Sabha polls. Eshwarappa also revealed that Karnataka BJP state president BY Vijayendra recently held discussions with his son, KE Kantesh, regarding the re-entry process.Stating that he will contest the upcoming assembly elections, Eshwarappa said a final decision on whether he himself or his son Kantesh will enter the race will be taken after further local consultations. Reaffirming his lifelong commitment to RSS ideology and the BJP, he ruled out joining any alternative political party, confirming he has turned down past proposals from Congress, Socialist Party, and Jana Sena Party. “My political journey began with the BJP, and I will remain committed to it until my last breath.
